seo.title: Adoption Visa (102) | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Adoption visa (subclass 102): Hague, expatriate and state adoptions, when the child visa is the better fit, and condition 8515.

hero.badge: Registered migration agents, Melbourne and Adelaide
intro: This visa allows children adopted overseas to move to Australia and live permanently with their adoptive parents.

blocks.x: The Adoption Visa (Subclass 102) allows a child outside Australia who has been, or is in the process of being, adopted by an Australian citizen, permanent resident, or eligible New Zealand citizen to live in Australia permanently. It helps unite families and gives the adopted child the same rights as any other permanent resident in Australia.
**What You Can Do with This Visa**

items.x: Live in Australia permanently.
Study and work without restriction.
Access Medicare and other benefits of permanent residency.
Sponsor eligible relatives for Australian visas.
Apply for Australian citizenship when eligible.
Travel freely to and from Australia for 5 years from visa grant.

blocks.x: **Eligibility**

items.x: The child must be under 18 when applying and when the visa is decided.
Must be outside Australia at both times.
Must be single (not married, engaged, or in a de facto relationship).
Must have a sponsor (adoptive parent) who is an Australian citizen, permanent resident, or eligible New Zealand citizen, aged 18 or older.
Must meet health and character requirements.

blocks.x: **How to Apply**

items.x: Confirm the adoption is legal and valid under Australian law.
Collect all required documents
Submit a paper application while the child is outside Australia.
From 23 July 2025, paper applications can be imported into Immi Account for tracking and document uploads.
Once approved, the child can move to Australia as a permanent resident.

sections.name: Which adoption
sections.h2: Three adoption situations, and one that is not this visa

blocks.x: Subclass 102 is a permanent visa for a child who is outside Australia and who has been, or is being, adopted by an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen. The child must be under 18 and single, both when you apply and when the visa is decided.
Australian authorities do not treat every overseas adoption as valid for migration. The pathway depends on how the adoption happened.

items.x: **Hague convention adoption.** The adoption is arranged between the central authorities of two Hague countries. Private arrangements made around the convention process usually do not qualify.

**Expatriate adoption.** You were living outside Australia for the required period and adopted the child under the law of that country. The Department looks at where you lived, how long you lived there, and whether the adoption gave you full and permanent parental rights.
**State or territory allocation.** A competent authority in Australia allocated the child for adoption. This is not a private family agreement.

blocks.x: If the child was already adopted before you became an Australian citizen or permanent resident, subclass 102 may be the wrong visa. The [child visa (101)](/family-visa/child-visa-subclass-101) is often the correct one. We check the dates of the adoption and of your status before you pay a charge.
A child who is adopted, or to be adopted, inside Australia is also a different process. Do not lodge a 102 for a child who is in Australia.

items.x: The adoption order or certificate, and evidence it is final if the visa requires a completed adoption.
Evidence the adoption was done through the right authority, not a private contract.
Proof of where the adoptive parent lived, for an expatriate adoption.
The child's passport, birth record and proof they are under 18 and single.
The sponsor's citizenship or permanent residence, and health and character checks when asked.

blocks.x: Translations must be complete. A partial translation of an adoption order is a common reason a file is delayed.

sections.name: Common refusal reasons
sections.h2: Common reasons these applications are refused

blocks.x: Adoption refusals are usually about the legal character of the adoption, not about how close the family feels.

items.x: **The adoption is not one Australia recognises for this visa.** Private adoptions, guardianship orders and temporary custody are the usual examples.
**The expatriate residence test is not met.** Short trips overseas do not replace a period of living in the country of adoption.
**The child is 18, married, engaged or in a de facto relationship.**
**The child is in Australia,** or the adoption was completed before the parent became a citizen or permanent resident and the child visa is the right subclass.
**Parental rights are shared or incomplete.** A simple guardianship order is not the same as a full adoption.

blocks.x: A refusal stays on your record. If you already have a refusal letter, read [visa refusal](/appeals/visa-refusal) and check the deadline before you reapply.
Subclass 102 is a permanent visa. After the child enters Australia they can live, study and work, and later apply for citizenship if they meet the residence rules.

items.x: **8515.** The child must not marry or start a de facto relationship before they enter Australia on this visa.
**Entry while the child is still under 18.** Plan travel so the child can enter in line with the grant. Tell us if the 18th birthday is close.
**Five-year travel facility.** After that, travel as a resident usually needs a [Resident Return visa](/bridging-return-visas/resident-return-visa-155-157).
**No employer condition.** This is not a work visa. Condition 8607 does not apply. The limit that matters before entry is 8515.

blocks.x: The numbers on your grant letter control what you can do. If a condition is breached, the visa can be cancelled. See [visa cancellation](/appeals/visa-cancellation) and, if you have a notice, [notice of intention to consider cancellation](/appeals/notice-of-intention-to-consider-cancellation).

items.x: [Child visa offshore (101)](/family-visa/child-visa-subclass-101)
[Orphan relative offshore (117)](/family-visa/orphan-relative-visa-117)
[Orphan relative onshore (837)](/family-visa/orphan-relative-visa-837)
[Family visas](/family-visa)

faqs.q: Can I adopt a relative's child and use this visa?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but only if the adoption itself meets Hague, expatriate or state-allocation rules. A family agreement or a guardianship order is often not enough. If the child is an orphan and a relative in Australia will care for them without that adoption, see the orphan relative visas.

faqs.q: We already adopted our child years ago, before I got permanent residence. Which visa is it?
faqs.a: Often the child visa (subclass 101), not the adoption visa. Bring the adoption date and the date you became a citizen or permanent resident.

faqs.q: Does the child have to stay outside Australia?
faqs.a: Yes for subclass 102. The child must be outside Australia when you apply and when the visa is decided.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee the adoption will be accepted?
faqs.a: No. Recognition of the adoption is a legal question, and only the Department decides the visa.

seo.title: DEPENDENT CHILD VISA | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Dependent child visa (subclass 445): a temporary visa for a child of a 309 or 820 holder, not a permanent child visa.

hero.badge: Registered migration agents, Melbourne and Adelaide
intro: The Subclass 445 visa lets a child stay in Australia while their parent’s Partner visa is processed.

blocks.x: The Dependent Child Visa (Subclass 445) lets a child of a parent who holds a temporary Partner visa stay in or move to Australia temporarily while their parent’s permanent Partner visa is being processed. It helps keep families together during the transition to permanent residency.
**What You Can Do with This Visa**

items.x: Live in Australia temporarily while the parent’s permanent Partner visa is under process.
Study and work in Australia.
Travel in and out of Australia freely while the visa is valid.
Later be added to the parent’s permanent Partner visa application to gain permanent residency.

blocks.x: **Eligibility**

items.x: Must be a dependent child of a parent who holds a temporary Partner visa.
Must be under 18, or over 18 and financially dependent on the parent.
Must meet health and character requirements.
The sponsoring parent must have lodged a valid permanent Partner visa application with the same sponsor for the child.

blocks.x: **How to Apply**

items.x: Check the child’s dependency and parent’s visa eligibility.
Gather all the supporting documents.
Lodge the application and complete health and character checks.
Wait for the decision; once granted, the child can live in Australia until the parent’s permanent Partner visa is finalized.
When the parent’s visa is approved, include the child in that application to gain permanent residence.

sections.name: What subclass 445 is
sections.h2: Subclass 445 is temporary, and it follows a partner visa

blocks.x: The dependent child visa (subclass 445) is not a permanent child visa and it is not a stand-alone way to sponsor your child. It lets a dependent child of a person who holds a temporary partner visa (subclass [309](/family-visa/partner-provisional-visa-subclass-309) or [820](/family-visa/partner-provisional-visa-subclass-820)) stay in, or come to, Australia while the parent's permanent partner visa is processed.

The parent must have made a valid application for the permanent partner visa ([100](/family-visa/partner-permanent-visa-subclass-100) or [801](/family-visa/partner-permanent-visa-subclass-801)) with the same sponsor. The child applies for the 445 so the family can be together during that wait. The 445 itself does not make the child a permanent resident.

When the parent's permanent partner visa is granted, the child needs to be included in that application, or otherwise hold a visa that gives them permanent residence. Families sometimes assume the 445 converts on its own. It does not. Tell us if the child was not declared on the original partner application. That fact changes the strategy.

Compare this with [subclass 101](/family-visa/child-visa-subclass-101) and [subclass 802](/family-visa/child-visa-subclass-802), which are for a child of an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen. If you are already a citizen or permanent resident, 445 is usually the wrong visa.

sections.name: Eligibility detail
sections.h2: Dependency, location and the parent's visa

items.x: **The parent holds 309 or 820.** A parent who only has a visitor visa, a prospective marriage visa, or no visa, cannot support a 445.

**The child is dependent.** Under 18 and single, or 18 or over and financially dependent in the way the partner visa rules require. A child who is married, engaged or de facto is not a dependent child.

**Location.** A 445 can be lodged for a child in Australia or outside Australia. The child's current visa still matters. Condition 8503 (no further stay) on a visitor visa can stop an onshore lodgement unless it is waived.
**Health and character.** Children 16 and over usually need police checks. Health examinations are requested by the Department.
**Same sponsor.** The permanent partner application and the 445 need to line up with the same sponsoring partner.

sections.name: Common refusal reasons
sections.h2: Common reasons these applications are refused

blocks.x: Most 445 problems come from using it as a general child visa, or from a partner application that did not include the child.

**The child is not a dependent child of that parent.** Step-children and children from a previous relationship need documents that show the legal relationship and dependency, not only photos.
**The child was never declared** on the partner application and there is no consistent explanation.
**The child has a partner,** works full time, or is not financially dependent.
**An onshore application is blocked** by condition 8503, 8534 or because the child does not hold a visa that allows a further application.

Subclass 445 is a temporary visa. It lasts only as long as the parent's temporary partner visa pathway allows. It is not permanent residence and it is not a skilled visa, so condition 8607 does not apply.

items.x: **Work and study.** A 445 holder can usually work and study in Australia. Check the grant letter. Do not assume a bridging visa granted earlier has the same rights.
**The visa ends.** If the parent's temporary partner visa ends, or the permanent partner visa is refused, the child's 445 does not keep them in Australia by itself.
**Permanent residence is a second step.** The child must be added to, or granted, the permanent partner visa. Budget for health checks again if the Department asks.
**8503 on the child's current visa.** If they are in Australia on a visa with no further stay, deal with the [waiver](/appeals/waiver-request) before you lodge.

faqs.a: No. 101 and 802 are permanent visas for the child of a citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen. 445 is a temporary visa for the child of a temporary partner visa holder.

faqs.q: Can the child stay forever on a 445?
faqs.a: No. They need to be included in the parent's permanent partner visa, or qualify for another permanent visa.

blocks.x: The **New Zealand Citizen Family Relationship visa (subclass 461)** is a **temporary visa** designed for individuals who are **not New Zealand citizens** but are members of the family unit of a New Zealand citizen who holds or is eligible for a Special Category visa (subclass 444).

This visa allows you to live, work, and study in Australia for up to 5 years, as well as travel in and out of Australia freely during its validity period. You can also apply for further subclass 461 visas to extend your stay, provided you continue to meet the eligibility requirements.

The subclass 461 visa is a great option for families wishing to live together in Australia, offering flexibility and access to key opportunities such as employment, education, and community participation while maintaining ties to New Zealand citizens residing in Australia.

hero.badge: Registered migration agents, Melbourne and Adelaide
intro: The Remaining Relative visa (Subclass 115) lets people with all close family in Australia live there permanently with their relatives.

blocks.x: The Remaining Relative visa (Subclass 115) is a permanent visa for people living outside Australia who have no close relatives outside the country. It allows them to join their only close family members who are Australian citizens, permanent residents, or eligible New Zealand citizens. This visa provides permanent residence but has very long processing times due to limited places each year.
**What You Can Do**

items.x: Live in Australia permanently.
Work and study in Australia.
Enrol in Australia’s public healthcare.
Travel freely for 5 years (then need Resident Return Visa or citizenship).
Sponsor relatives to come to Australia.

blocks.x: **Eligibility**

items.x: Applicant and partner must have no other near relatives outside Australia.
Must have an eligible sponsor (Australian citizen/PR/eligible NZ citizen) who is a close relative and settled in Australia.
Assurance of Support required.
Must meet health and character requirements.
Must be offshore at both lodgement and grant.

blocks.x: **How to Apply**

items.x: Check eligibility and confirm sponsor.
Gather all the supporting documents for your application.
Lodge application offshore and pay fees.
Receive queue date and wait until your place is released.
After receiving the grant, migrate, live, and work in Australia permanently.

Subclass 115 is a permanent visa for a person outside Australia whose near relatives usually live in Australia. You must be outside Australia when you lodge and when the visa is granted. If you are in Australia, read [subclass 835](/family-visa/remaining-relative-visa-subclass-835) instead, and check whether your current visa lets you apply.

A near relative is a partner, parent, child or sibling, including step-relationships of those types. Your partner's near relatives are counted as well. The test is about where those people usually live, not about who you feel closest to.

items.x: A near relative who is an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen and who usually lives in Australia does not stop you.
A near relative who usually lives outside Australia does stop you. One parent, one sibling or one adult child overseas is enough.
A near relative who is in Australia on a temporary visa is usually treated as not settled here, so they can also stop you.
A partner, spouse or de facto, is included in the picture. You cannot qualify by leaving them off the form.

blocks.x: The sponsor must be a settled Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen, and must be your near relative (or your partner's, in the way the rules allow). Settled usually means lawfully resident in Australia for a reasonable period. Two years is the figure case officers often use. It is not a promise that two years is always enough, or that less is always fatal.

These visas are capped. There are more applicants than places, so a complete file can still wait years for a queue place. We will tell you, before you pay, if another visa is more realistic. The [family visa overview](/family-visa) compares the options.

Before a 115 is granted, an Assurance of Support is usually required. That is a legal promise, often backed by a bond, that the assurer will support you so you do not rely on certain social security payments. The bond is held for a set period. It is separate from the visa application charge and it is not our professional fee.
Start collecting evidence of every near relative and where they live. A statutory declaration that says "I have no family overseas" is not enough if a sibling's address turns up in other records.

items.x: Identity documents for you, your partner and any dependent children.
Evidence of where each parent, sibling and child lives, including people you have little contact with.
The sponsor's citizenship or permanent residence, and evidence they are settled.
Police checks and health examinations when the Department asks.

sections.h2: Common reasons these applications are refused

blocks.x: Remaining relative refusals are mostly about a relative the applicant hoped would not count.

items.x: **A near relative lives outside Australia,** including a sibling you no longer speak to, or your partner's parent.
**A near relative is in Australia on a temporary visa,** so they are not usually resident as a citizen or permanent resident.
**The sponsor is not settled,** or is a cousin, aunt or friend. Those relationships do not meet the sponsor test for this visa.
**You are in Australia when you lodge or when a decision is ready.** Subclass 115 cannot be granted onshore.
**The Assurance of Support is not provided** when the Department asks, or the assurer does not meet the income test.

blocks.x: A refusal stays on your record. If you already have a refusal letter, read [visa refusal](/appeals/visa-refusal) and check the deadline before you reapply.
Subclass 115 is a permanent visa. You wait offshore, so you do not get a bridging visa for this application. After grant you can live, work and study in Australia.

items.x: **No work condition after grant.** Condition 8607 does not apply. You are not tied to an employer.
**Travel facility.** Usually five years from grant, then a [Resident Return visa](/bridging-return-visas/resident-return-visa-155-157) if you want to travel as a resident.
**You cannot move to Australia while you wait.** Plan where you will live during a long queue. Visiting Australia on a visitor visa does not convert this application into an onshore visa.
**Condition 8503** on a later visitor visa can stop you lodging a different visa in Australia. It does not remove the need to be offshore for the 115 itself.

blocks.x: The numbers on your grant letter control what you can do. If a condition is breached, the visa can be cancelled. See [visa cancellation](/appeals/visa-cancellation) and, if you have a notice, [notice of intention to consider cancellation](/appeals/notice-of-intention-to-consider-cancellation).

faqs.a: You are unlikely to be a remaining relative. The test does not ignore relatives you are estranged from.

faqs.q: Can I wait in Australia?
faqs.a: Not on a subclass 115. You must be outside Australia at lodgement and at grant. Subclass 835 is the onshore visa, and your current visa has to allow that application.

faqs.q: How long is the queue?
faqs.a: Places are limited and the wait is long. We will not guess a grant date. Check the Department's figures before you pay the charge.

faqs.q: Is an Assurance of Support the same as sponsorship?
faqs.a: No. Sponsorship is the relative who supports the application. The Assurance of Support is a separate financial bond and legal promise, and it is usually required before grant.

faqs.q: Will you guarantee the visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department decides.

sections.name: Who is an orphan relative
sections.h2: When subclass 117 is the right visa

blocks.x: Subclass 117 is a permanent visa for a child who is outside Australia and who cannot be cared for by either parent. The child must be under 18 and single when you apply and when the visa is decided, and must be outside Australia at both times. A child already in Australia looks at [subclass 837](/family-visa/orphan-relative-visa-837).

Both parents must be dead, or their whereabouts must be unknown, or they must be permanently unable to care for the child because of a physical or mental incapacity. One parent who is alive and able to care for the child, even if they are unwilling, usually means this visa is not available. A parent who could sponsor the child as their own child is a [child visa](/family-visa/child-visa-subclass-101) case, not an orphan relative case.

The sponsor must be a settled Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen, and a relative of the child: a brother, sister, grandparent, aunt, uncle, niece or nephew, including step-relationships of those kinds. A cousin is not enough. The sponsor has to be able to look after the child. This visa is not a way to adopt a child outside the adoption rules. If you are adopting, read the [adoption visa](/family-visa/adoption-visa).

sections.name: Evidence
sections.h2: Evidence of the parents and of the relationship

items.x: The child's birth certificate and the documents that link them to the sponsor (for example, the parent's birth certificate and the sponsor's birth certificate, so the aunt or uncle relationship is clear).
Death certificates of the parents, or police or court records that their whereabouts are unknown, or medical evidence that a parent is permanently incapacitated.
Evidence no other parent has parental responsibility.
The sponsor's status in Australia and evidence they can house and support the child.
Health examinations and, if the child is 16 or over, character documents.

blocks.x: Paper applications for this visa can be imported into ImmiAccount in the circumstances the Department allows. Importing a file does not by itself make a child eligible.

sections.name: Common refusal reasons
sections.h2: Common reasons these applications are refused

blocks.x: Orphan relative cases are refused when the parent test or the relationship test is not met, even if the child genuinely needs help.

items.x: **A parent is alive and able to care,** including a parent who is overseas and simply does not want to.
**The sponsor is not the right relative,** such as a cousin, family friend or a parent who should be using a child visa.
**The child is 18, engaged, married or de facto.**
**The child is in Australia.** Subclass 117 cannot be granted onshore.
**The relationship documents do not connect** the child to the sponsor. A single affidavit from the family is rarely enough.
**The order is guardianship, not a situation where the parents cannot care.** Guardianship alone does not create an orphan relative.

**Not a work visa.** There is no condition 8607. The condition that matters before travel is 8515.

seo.title: Carer visa Offshore (subclass 116) | Carer Visa Sub Class 116 | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Offshore Carer visa (subclass 116): the two-year care test, why other relatives in Australia matter, and the long capped queue.

hero.badge: Registered migration agents, Melbourne and Adelaide
intro: This permanent visa lets you move to Australia to care for someone with a long-term medical condition. They must have no reasonable access to care options in Australia.

blocks.x: The Carer Visa (Subclass 116) is a permanent visa for people outside Australia who want to move and provide ongoing, substantial care for a relative in Australia with a long-term medical condition. It is intended for situations where the person in Australia cannot get the necessary care from other family members, hospitals, or welfare services.
**What You Can Do with This Visa**

items.x: Live in Australia permanently and can work and study without any limitations.
Access Australia’s Medicare (public healthcare).
Sponsor eligible family members to join you in Australia.
Apply for Australian citizenship when eligible.

blocks.x: **Eligibility**

items.x: You must be outside Australia at the time of application and visa grant.
You must be able and willing to provide long-term care.
The person needing care must be an Australian citizen, permanent resident, or eligible New Zealand citizen with a verified medical condition.
You and any family members who are applying for this visa must meet health requirements.
You must be sponsored by your relative or their partner.

blocks.x: **How to Apply**

items.x: Confirm that you and your sponsor meet all eligibility criteria.
Obtain a medical assessment confirming your relative’s need for care.
Prepare and submit your application from outside Australia with all required documents (identity, sponsorship, health, and care evidence).
Pay the visa fee and wait for the Department of Home Affairs to process your application.
Once granted, you can move permanently to Australia to care for your relative.

sections.name: The care test
sections.h2: The medical test is the centre of this visa

blocks.x: Subclass 116 is a permanent visa for a person who will give substantial, ongoing care to an Australian relative, or to a member of that relative's family unit. You must be outside Australia when you apply and when the visa is granted. The other location uses [subclass 836](/family-visa/carer-visa-onshore-subclass-836).

The person who needs care must be an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen, usually living in Australia. They need a medical assessment through the provider the Department uses. The certificate has to show a medical condition that will continue for at least two years, a need for direct assistance with the practical parts of daily life, and that the assistance cannot reasonably be obtained from another relative in Australia or from hospitals, nursing homes, or community and welfare services.

"No one else will do it" is not the test. If a sibling in Australia could reasonably help, or if community care is available, the certificate will often say the care need is not met for this visa. Families are disappointed when they pay for the medical assessment and the result is negative. We talk through that risk first.

You must be a relative of the right class: partner, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, aunt, uncle, niece or nephew, including step-relationships. A cousin or a close friend does not qualify. You must be willing and able to give the care. Your own health can be a reason the Department finds you cannot.

These visas are capped. There are more applicants than places, so a complete file can still wait years for a queue place. We will tell you, before you pay, if another visa is more realistic. The [family visa overview](/family-visa) compares the options.

sections.name: Evidence
sections.h2: Sponsorship, assessment and Assurance of Support

items.x: The carer visa medical assessment for the person who needs care. Do not substitute a GP letter and assume it replaces the official assessment.
Evidence of the family relationship between you and the person in Australia.
A statement of the care you will provide, and why other relatives in Australia cannot provide it. Name those relatives. Do not leave them off.
The sponsor's citizenship or residence. The sponsor is usually the person who needs care, or their partner.
Health and character checks for you and any family members included in the application.

blocks.x: An Assurance of Support is commonly required before grant. It is a bond and a legal promise, separate from the visa application charge. Charges on this page are from the Department of Home Affairs pricing table and can change, usually on 1 July. Check the [current visa pricing table](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/fees-and-charges/current-visa-pricing) before you pay.

sections.name: Common refusal reasons
sections.h2: Common reasons these applications are refused

blocks.x: Carer visas are refused on the availability of care in Australia more often than on the diagnosis itself.

items.x: **The medical assessment does not support the visa.** The condition may be serious and still fail the two-year or "care not available in Australia" tests.
**Another relative in Australia could reasonably provide the care,** even if the family prefers you.
**You are not a relative of the class the visa allows,** or the person who needs care is not an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen.
**You are in Australia** at lodgement or decision. Subclass 116 is refused or invalid if you are onshore. Use subclass 836 only if your visa allows that application.
**You cannot provide the care** because of your own health, work plans or because you will not actually live with or near the person.
**The Assurance of Support** is not lodged by an assurer who meets the income test.

blocks.x: A refusal stays on your record. If you already have a refusal letter, read [visa refusal](/appeals/visa-refusal) and check the deadline before you reapply.
Subclass 116 is permanent. You stay outside Australia until it is granted. There is no bridging visa for an offshore carer application.

items.x: **After grant** you can live, work and study in Australia. Condition 8607 does not apply. You are not tied to an employer, but you have told the Department you will provide the care. If you never do, the visa can be at risk and later applications will ask what happened.
**Travel facility.** Usually five years, then a [Resident Return visa](/bridging-return-visas/resident-return-visa-155-157).
**You cannot move early.** A visitor visa while you wait does not turn a 116 into an onshore application. Condition 8503 on that visitor visa can also stop a later onshore lodgement.
**Family members** included on the application must meet health and character rules. Their needs do not replace the care test.

blocks.x: The numbers on your grant letter control what you can do. If a condition is breached, the visa can be cancelled. See [visa cancellation](/appeals/visa-cancellation) and, if you have a notice, [notice of intention to consider cancellation](/appeals/notice-of-intention-to-consider-cancellation).

faqs.q: Who does the medical assessment?
faqs.a: The Department's approved provider, not your local doctor. A specialist report can support the file, but it does not replace the carer assessment certificate.

faqs.q: Can I apply if my parent already has a home-care package?
faqs.a: You can apply, but existing community care is often the reason the assessment finds that assistance can be obtained in Australia. We look at that before you pay.

faqs.q: Can I wait in Australia?
faqs.a: Not on subclass 116. You must be offshore at application and grant.

faqs.q: Is the queue short because the need is medical?
faqs.a: No. Carer visas are capped. Medical need does not jump the queue.

faqs.q: Will you guarantee the visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department decides, and the medical assessment is a separate step that can stop the case.

seo.h1: Aged Dependent Relative Visa: Which Subclass Applies to Your Relative?

hero.badge: Registered migration agents, Melbourne and Adelaide
hero.h1: Aged Dependent Relative Visa: Which Subclass Applies to Your Relative?
intro: The Aged Dependent Relative visa is for an older person who depends on a relative in Australia. There are two subclasses: 114 for people overseas and 838 for people already in Australia. This page helps you pick the right one.

sections.name: What this visa family is
sections.h2: Two visas, one question: where is your relative?

blocks.x: The Aged Dependent Relative visa is for an older person who is single and relies on a relative in Australia. These are not general parent visas. If the older person is your parent, [check the parent visa options](/family-visa) first.
The detailed requirements, costs, process and documents are on the page for each visa. This page only helps you choose.

head: Your relative is
Visa
What changes
Detailed page
rows: They wait overseas and the sponsor's evidence of support is central
Their current visa and bridging visa matter from the first day

blocks.x: The location when you lodge decides which visa applies. Not sure? [Book a consultation](/book-an-appointment) and bring your relative's passport and visa details.

An aged dependent relative is not a parent visa and not a remaining relative visa. It is for an older relative who has relied on you for the basic needs of life for a substantial period, and who has no partner. If the person is your parent, start with the [parent visas on the family page](/family-visa). The balance of family test and the contributory charges are a different system.

items.x: **Age.** They must be old enough to be granted an Australian age pension. For most people that age is 67. Check Services Australia for the age that applies to their date of birth.
**Single.** They are widowed, divorced, separated or never married. A person who still has a partner usually does not qualify.
**Dependent.** For a reasonable period, commonly looked at over about three years, they have depended on you for food, clothing and shelter more than on anyone else or on their own income.

**Relationship.** You are a settled Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen, and you are their child, sibling, parent, grandparent, grandchild, aunt, uncle, niece or nephew (including step-relationships).

**Where they are.** Outside Australia is [subclass 114](/family-visa/aged-dependent-offshore-114). In Australia is [subclass 838](/family-visa/aged-dependent-onshore-838). The location at lodgement decides the subclass.

blocks.x: Both visas are permanent and both are capped. The wait for a place can be many years. An Assurance of Support is usually required before grant. Paying the visa application charge does not speed the queue up.

If they are in Australia, read the visa conditions on the visa they hold now. Condition 8503 (no further stay) can stop an onshore application. If they are outside Australia, they stay outside until a 114 is granted.

sections.name: Choosing
sections.h2: How to choose, and reasons these cases fail

blocks.x: Bring their age, marital status, a simple picture of who has paid their rent and food, and where every close relative lives. We would rather tell you the test fails than lodge a capped visa that cannot be granted.

items.x: **They are still married or de facto,** even if the partner lives elsewhere.
**They support themselves** with a pension, rent or work, and your help is extra rather than their main support.
**The dependence is recent.** A few months of help after a crisis is often not the reasonable period the visa requires.
**They are your parent.** A parent visa may be open, or it may be closed by the balance of family test. Guessing wrong is expensive.
**The sponsor is not settled,** or the relationship is a cousin or a friend.

blocks.x: The granted visa is permanent. Conditions bite earlier, while you wait, and they depend on which subclass you use.

items.x: **Subclass 114.** The relative waits offshore. There is no bridging visa. After grant they can work and study. Travel is usually for five years, then a [Resident Return visa](/bridging-return-visas/resident-return-visa-155-157). There is no condition 8607.

**Subclass 838.** They wait in Australia on a bridging visa if they get one. That visa may have condition 8101 (no work). They must not leave if the bridging visa does not allow travel, and they must be in Australia when the visa is decided.
**8503.** A no-further-stay condition on a current visa can stop the 838 from being lodged. It does not apply to the permanent visa after grant.
**Assurance of Support.** This is a condition of the process before grant, not a schedule 8 visa condition. Budget for the bond separately from the application charge.

blocks.x: The numbers on your grant letter control what you can do. If a condition is breached, the visa can be cancelled. See [visa cancellation](/appeals/visa-cancellation) and, if you have a notice, [notice of intention to consider cancellation](/appeals/notice-of-intention-to-consider-cancellation).

faqs.q: Is this the same as a parent visa?
faqs.a: No. It is a separate visa for an older dependent relative. A parent visa has its own tests and costs.

faqs.q: Can my aunt or uncle apply?
faqs.a: They may, if they meet the relationship and dependency rules.

faqs.q: Is it a permanent visa?
faqs.a: Yes.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee the visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department decides.

faqs.q: Is this visa for my mother or father?
faqs.a: Usually no. Parents use parent visas. Use this visa only when the relative is not your parent, or when we have checked that a parent visa is not the right class.

faqs.q: What age do they need to be?
faqs.a: Old enough for the Australian age pension. That is 67 for people born on or after 1 January 1957. Confirm the age for their birth date.

faqs.q: Can a married aunt apply?
faqs.a: Not while she has a partner. The applicant has to be single.

faqs.q: Which subclass do we use?
faqs.a: 114 if they are outside Australia. 838 if they are in Australia and their current visa lets them apply.

faqs.q: Will you guarantee a place in the queue?
faqs.a: No. Places are capped and only the Department decides.

blocks.x: The Aged Dependent Relative Visa (Subclass 838) is a permanent residency visa designed for single, older individuals who rely on a relative in Australia for financial support. This visa allows you to live permanently in Australia, sponsor eligible relatives, and apply for Australian citizenship if you meet the eligibility criteria.
Benefits of the Aged Dependent Relative Visa (Subclass 838)
The Subclass 838 visa offers numerous benefits, including:

items.x: Live and work freely: Reside and work anywhere in Australia without restrictions.
Indefinite residency: Renew your 5-year visa multiple times with no limitations.
Family sponsorship: Sponsor eligible relatives to join you in Australia.

blocks.x: Eligibility Requirements for the Aged Dependent Relative Visa (Subclass 838)
To qualify for this visa, you must meet the following criteria:

items.x: Location Requirement: You must be in Australia (but not in immigration clearance) when you apply for this visa and when the Department makes a decision.
Sponsorship: You must be sponsored by an eligible relative or their partner who is an Australian citizen, permanent resident, or eligible New Zealand citizen.
Age Requirement: You must meet the minimum age to qualify for the Australian age pension.

Financial Dependence: You must have been financially dependent on your Australian relative for basic needs (e.g., food, shelter, clothing) for at least 3 years before applying. Financial dependence may also be due to a disability that prevents you from working.
Marital Status: You must not have a partner or spouse.
Visa Conditions: Your current visa must not include a no further stay condition .
Assurance of Support: You must be able to obtain an assurance of support from your sponsor.
Health and Character Requirements: You and any accompanying family members must meet the health and character requirements set by the Department of Home Affairs.
Outstanding Debts: Any debts owed to the Australian Government by you or your family members must be paid or arrangements must be in place to repay them.
Previous Visa Issues: You may not be eligible if you have had a visa refused or canceled while in Australia.

sections.name: What decides a visitor visa
sections.h2: The test behind every visitor visa

blocks.x: The Department of Home Affairs must be satisfied that you intend to visit Australia temporarily and then leave. This is the genuine temporary stay test in clause 600.211 of Schedule 2 to the Migration Regulations. The decision maker looks at your whole situation. No single document guarantees a grant.

head: What they look at
Evidence that helps
rows: Employer letter with approved leave and return date, recent payslips and tax returns, business registration if self-employed, proof of study
Recent bank statements showing steady funds, an explanation for any large or recent deposits, evidence of assets
Close family who stay at home, a travel history that shows you followed visa conditions

sections.name: Conditions to know
sections.h2: Visa conditions that catch visitors out

items.x: **Condition 8101 (no work).** You cannot work in Australia on a standard visitor visa.
**Condition 8201 (study limit).** Study is limited to 3 months.
**Condition 8503 (no further stay).** You cannot apply for most other visas while you are in Australia. A waiver is only given in limited, compelling cases.
**Condition 8558 (stay limit).** You cannot stay more than 12 months in any 18-month period.

blocks.x: Breaking a condition can lead to cancellation and make later visa applications harder. Check your grant letter for the conditions on your visa.

sections.h2: Common reasons visitor visas are refused

items.x: Weak ties to home, such as no job, no leave approval or no close family there.
Savings that do not match the trip, or unexplained deposits.
A vague itinerary, or one that does not match the stated purpose.
A history of overstays, refusals or breaches that was not explained.
A sponsor or host who has not shown their own status or relationship.
Answers on the form that do not match your documents.

blocks.x: A refusal stays on your record and is asked about in later applications. If you were refused, read our [visa refusal page](/appeals/visa-refusal) before you reapply. faqs.q: Which visa do I need to visit Australia?
faqs.a: It depends on your passport and purpose. Some passport holders can use an ETA (601) or eVisitor (651). Others apply for a visitor visa (600). Young people from eligible countries may use a working holiday or work and holiday visa.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ETA 601 and eVisitor 651?
faqs.a: Both are quick online authorities for short visits. The ETA is for eligible non-European passports and is applied for by app, with a service charge. The eVisitor is free and for eligible European passports.

faqs.q: How long can I stay on a visitor visa?
faqs.a: It depends on the visa granted. ETA and eVisitor allow up to 3 months per visit. A 600 is usually granted for 3, 6 or 12 months. Condition 8558 may also limit total time.

faqs.q: Can I work on a visitor visa?
faqs.a: No. Visitor visas carry condition 8101. Business visitors can attend meetings and conferences, but they cannot do productive work or sell services to the public.

faqs.q: Can my parents visit me in Melbourne?
faqs.a: Yes, usually on a visitor visa (600). If you are an Australian citizen or permanent resident, you may sponsor them under the Sponsored Family stream. Our Sponsored Family guide explains what you need.

faqs.q: Can I extend my visitor visa?
faqs.a: Not in the usual sense. You apply for a new visitor visa before your current one ends, and condition 8503 may stop you. See our onshore visitor visa extension page.

faqs.q: How long does a visitor visa take?
faqs.a: Processing times change often. Check the Department's current global processing times before you plan.

faqs.q: Why was my visitor visa refused?
faqs.a: The most common reason is that the Department was not satisfied you would leave Australia. Book a consultation so we can read your refusal letter and explain your options.

faqs.q: Does each family member need their own application?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Each traveller, including children, needs their own visa or authority. Check the Department of Home Affairs website for how to apply for children, or ask us.

cta.title: Not sure which visa fits your trip?
cta.text: Tell us your passport, plans and any past visa history. We will tell you the right visa and what evidence you need.

faqs.q: Can I extend my tourist visa from overseas?
faqs.a: No. You apply for a new visa. Each application is a fresh decision.

faqs.q: How soon can I come back to Australia?
faqs.a: It depends on your visa conditions and your history. Condition 8558 limits total stay in any 18-month period.

faqs.q: Can I apply for an ETA or eVisitor again?
faqs.a: If your passport is eligible, yes. The ETA or eVisitor lets you stay up to 3 months per visit.

faqs.q: Will a refusal affect a new application?
faqs.a: Yes. It is recorded and must be declared on later forms.

faqs.q: Can I work on a visitor visa?
faqs.a: No.

faqs.q: Is the Sponsored Family stream for repeat visits?
faqs.a: It can be used for visits, but it is not designed for long or frequent stays.

faqs.q: What if my visa is about to end and I am in Australia?
faqs.a: Read our onshore visitor visa extension page.

seo.title: Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) Review | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: The Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) can review certain Australian immigration, refugee protection, character-related visa, citizenship, nomination.

intro: The Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) can review certain Australian immigration, refugee protection, character-related visa, citizenship, nomination, and sponsorship decisions made by the Department of Home Affairs or the relevant Ministers. It helps people who disagree with a decision seek a merits review.

blocks.x: What the Tribunal can review

The ART can review some though not all decisions made by the Department of Home Affairs and the Ministers for Home Affairs and Immigration. These include refusals and cancellations across visas and citizenship, as well as employer-related decisions like nominations and sponsorships.
Migration visa refusals or cancellations

If your application for a migration visa was refused, or your visa was cancelled, you may be able to ask the Tribunal to reconsider the decision. This can apply to various visa subclasses and circumstances depending on eligibility and time limits.
Protection (refugee) visa refusals or cancellations

Applicants whose protection (refugee) visas are refused or cancelled can seek review. The Tribunal reassesses the merits of the case, considering country information and any new relevant evidence permitted by law.
Character-related visa decisions

Where a visa is refused or cancelled on character grounds (for example, under section 501 of the Migration Act), the ART may review the decision. Reviews assess whether the original decision was the correct and preferable one in light of the evidence.
Australian citizenship refusals or cancellations

If your citizenship application was refused, or your citizenship was cancelled, you may be eligible for Tribunal review. The ART examines the decision against relevant criteria, including good character and residency requirements.
Nomination refusals

Employers and applicants can seek review of decisions refusing the nomination of an occupation, activity, or position associated with employer-sponsored visas. The Tribunal considers whether the nominated role and employer meet the program’s requirements.
Sponsorship decisions
The ART can review decisions to bar a sponsor, refuse to approve a sponsorship, or cancel an existing approval. This provides sponsors an avenue to challenge findings and present supporting evidence.
Applying, managing your case, and daily listings

You can apply for a review online, manage your case through the ART portal, and check daily listings to see hearing schedules and outcomes. Strict application deadlines apply refer to your decision notice for the time limit.
Language help and website translation

The website offers a translation feature for people who speak languages other than English. Important notes about accuracy and limitations are provided before using this tool to ensure you understand critical information.
Acknowledgement of Country

The Administrative Review Tribunal acknowledges the Traditional Owners and Custodians of Country throughout Australia, recognizing their ongoing connection to land, waters, and communities, and paying respects to Elders past and present.

The Administrative Review Tribunal can review some decisions of the Department and of the Minister's delegates. In a merits review the Tribunal asks whether the correct decision is to grant, refuse or cancel, on the material before it. That is wider than a court, which looks only at legal error. It is narrower than people hope: the Tribunal can only review decisions the Migration Act lists, and it cannot grant a visa the law does not allow.

items.x: **Many onshore visa refusals and cancellations** can be reviewed. Many offshore refusals cannot.
**Protection visa decisions** have their own rules, deadlines and divisions. Do not use a visitor-visa checklist for a protection case.
**Character decisions under section 501** can be reviewable when a delegate made them. A decision the Minister made personally often cannot.
**Sponsorship, nomination and citizenship decisions** are reviewable only where the Act says so. A disappointed employer does not automatically have a review.

blocks.x: You apply online through the Tribunal, pay the fee, and then the case is either decided on the papers or listed for a hearing. You can usually send new evidence. New evidence should answer the reason for refusal. A second copy of the original file does not.

If the Tribunal affirms the decision, we explain whether a lawyer should look at a judicial review, and the short time you have to file.

seo.title: Federal Court Migration Appeals Guidance | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Guidance from the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia on appealing migration decisions to the Federal Court. An appeal challenges legal errors.

intro: Guidance from the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia on appealing migration decisions to the Federal Court. An appeal challenges legal errors in the original judgment; it is not a re-hearing and generally involves no new evidence.

blocks.x: What is a migration appeal?

An appeal asks the Federal Court to set aside a decision because the original Judge made a legal error. Appeals are usually heard by a single Judge, unless referred to a Full Court (three Judges). The appeal focuses on whether the law was applied correctly, not on re-deciding visa outcomes.
What the appeal Judge does and does not do

items.x: Does not decide whether a visa should be granted or cancelled.
Does not consider new evidence (except in special circumstances).
Does not call new witnesses.
Does read the documents filed in the original case and relevant transcript.
Does hear legal arguments from both parties.

blocks.x: What you must prove to succeed
You must show a significant legal mistake in the original decision (for example, applying the wrong legal principle) that justifies overturning the outcome.
If the Minister appeals
If you won your review, the Minister may appeal. You will receive a notice of appeal and become the respondent.
Legal advice and representation
You are strongly encouraged to obtain legal advice before appealing. Court staff cannot provide legal advice. A lawyer can:

items.x: Assess whether you have appealable legal issues.
Explain options, procedures, and likely costs.
Help draft a technically correct notice of appeal.

blocks.x: If you do not have a lawyer, free or low‑cost legal assistance may be available through community legal organisations.
Costs and fees
Appeals can be expensive. You must pay:

items.x: A filing fee when lodging the notice of appeal.
A separate setting‑down fee. If you lose, you may be ordered to pay the Minister’s legal costs.

blocks.x: Drafting the notice of appeal
Success depends on showing how the law should have been interpreted. Drafting grounds is technical and difficult, so legal assistance is recommended.
Additional resources and support

items.x: Federal Court website has more information about appeals.
Interpreters and accessibility support are available.
If documents were destroyed in a natural disaster, you can request replacements at no cost using the Natural disaster replacement document request form.

sections.name: Legal error
sections.h2: The court does not re-hear your visa

blocks.x: A judicial review asks a judge whether the decision-maker misunderstood the law, ignored evidence it had to consider, or reached a decision no reasonable decision-maker could reach. It does not ask whether the judge would have granted the visa. A strong relationship, a sick child or a job offer does not matter unless the Tribunal was legally required to take it into account and did not.

Migration judicial review is usually filed in the Federal Circuit and Family Court, with some cases going to the Federal Court. The time limit is short. For many migration decisions it is 35 days from the date of the decision, and an extension is not routine. Count from the decision, not from the day you decided to get advice.

If you lose, costs can be ordered against you. That risk is a reason to get a lawyer's opinion before you file, not after. Court staff cannot advise you. Community legal centres may help if you are eligible.

sections.name: Agents and lawyers
sections.h2: What we do, and what a lawyer does

blocks.x: Bansal Immigration is a migration agency. Registered migration agents do not appear as counsel and do not file judicial review applications as your lawyer. What we do is read the Tribunal's reasons, tell you whether we can see an arguable legal error, and help you brief a lawyer while the 35 days are still open.

items.x: We gather the decision, the review papers and the chronology a lawyer will ask for.
We explain the difference between "I disagree" and "the Tribunal applied the wrong test".
We tell you if we do not see a legal error. Filing because you are unhappy is how people pay two sets of costs.
If the Minister appeals a decision you won, you need a lawyer quickly. The notice of appeal has its own deadline.

faqs.q: Will the court grant my visa?
faqs.a: No. If you win, the usual order is that the Tribunal or the Department must decide the matter again according to law. A new decision can still be a refusal.

seo.title: Ministerial Intervention Australia | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Ministerial Intervention under sections 351 and 501J of the Migration Act 1958 allows the Australian Immigration Minister to personally consider granting.

intro: Ministerial Intervention under sections 351 and 501J of the Migration Act 1958 allows the Australian Immigration Minister to personally consider granting a visa to let a person stay in Australia, overriding certain tribunal decisions if it is in the public interest. This process is discretionary, non-compellable, and requires a prior merits review tribunal decision.

blocks.x: Overview of Ministerial Intervention

Ministerial Intervention is a special discretionary power where the Minister for Immigration may grant a visa despite an adverse decision by a merits review tribunal. The Minister can replace a tribunal’s decision with a more favorable one if it is deemed in the public interest. This power is personal to the Minister and cannot be delegated or compelled. Requests for intervention are not part of the standard visa application process and are considered only after a tribunal decision.
Legislative basis and powers

The Minister’s powers come from sections 351 and 501J of the Migration Act 1958. Although section 417 was repealed, the Minister can still exercise intervention powers under section 351, including cases previously covered by section 417. The Minister’s intervention decisions are final and not subject to automatic review.
Personal Procedural Decisions (PPDs)

On 4 September 2025, the Minister issued Personal Procedural Decisions under sections 351 and 501J, setting criteria for which requests will be personally considered. Requests lodged before 12 April 2023 or not meeting criteria may be finalized by the Department without Ministerial consideration. New requests can be made and will be assessed against updated Ministerial Instructions.
When you can make a request

You can request Ministerial Intervention only if you have a decision from the Administrative Review Tribunal or Administrative Appeals Tribunal. The Minister’s powers do not apply if there is no tribunal decision, if the Minister has already intervened, if a court has quashed the decision, or if the tribunal has returned the case for reconsideration and a new decision has been made.
Who can make a request

You or your authorised representative can submit a request. Without your authority, the Department will not communicate with third parties. Authorised representatives must complete the appropriate forms (Form 956 or Form 956A).
Including family members
Family members can only be included in a request if they also have a merits review tribunal decision.
Criteria for referral
Requests are assessed against criteria outlined in section 13 of the Ministerial Instructions. Only requests meeting these criteria will be referred to the Minister for consideration.
How to make a request

Requests must be made in writing, either online via the Contact the Minister form or by post to the Minister for Immigration and Citizenship at Parliament House, Canberra. The request must clearly identify who is included, specify the intervention powers relied upon, reference the tribunal decision, state the relevant section 13 criteria, and provide all supporting information.
Providing certified documents

Certified copies of supporting documents should be provided with the request. Certification must be done by authorised persons such as magistrates, Justices of the Peace, solicitors, or other listed officials. Documents not in English must be accompanied by accredited English translations.
Additional information and actions

If your request meets referral criteria, you may be asked to provide further information such as health examinations, police clearances, or proof of family member citizenship within a specified timeframe.
Important notes

Do not send electronic devices (USBs, CDs) as they will not be accessed and will be returned. The Minister is not obliged to consider all requests, and there are no guaranteed timeframes for decisions.

sections.name: Not a right
sections.h2: The Minister does not have to consider your request

blocks.x: Ministerial intervention is not an appeal. Under sections 351 and 501J of the Migration Act the Minister may, personally, substitute a more favourable decision after a merits review tribunal has decided the case. The Minister does not have to look at the request, does not have to give reasons if they do not intervene, and does not have to decide it within any time you can plan around.

You generally cannot ask until the Tribunal has made a decision. A Department refusal that was never reviewed is not a ministerial case. Section 417, which people still mention, is not the power to rely on. Follow the current ministerial instructions. The Minister has published guidelines about which requests are even referred.

Unique or exceptional circumstances are the usual threshold: compelling compassionate factors that were not, and could not have been, dealt with by the Tribunal applying the ordinary criteria. A repeat of the visa application, or disagreement with the Tribunal, is not intervention.

sections.name: How a request is made
sections.h2: How a request is actually made

items.x: You need the tribunal decision, and only people covered by that decision can be included.
The request is in writing, by the Department's form or by post, as the current instructions require. Unsigned emails and USB sticks are not a request.
Documents should be certified copies if the instructions ask for them.
If the Department asks for health or police checks, the deadline in that letter matters. A request can be closed if you do not answer.
There is no ART review of a decision not to intervene. Judicial review is limited and is a matter for a lawyer.

sections.h2: How we help with a request

blocks.x: We first say if a request is even available. If you still have a Tribunal deadline, we deal with that first. Intervention is not a backup you can keep in your pocket while a review clock runs out.

If a request is available, we help you gather the circumstances that are actually outside the visa criteria: medical evidence, the situation of a child, or a factor the Tribunal had no power to weigh. We do not promise that the Minister will see the file.

seo.title: Overview of Immigration Review Process | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: How an Australian visa review moves from your decision letter to the ART, the courts and the Minister. Deadlines are short. Call Bansal Immigration.

intro: A visa review is a sequence of steps, and each step has its own deadline. Start with the date in your decision letter, then work out whether the Administrative Review Tribunal, a court or the Minister is the right next step.

blocks.x: How a review usually unfolds

After the Department of Home Affairs refuses or cancels a visa, your review rights depend on the decision and where you are. Your letter says whether you can ask for review, who decides it and how long you have. Time is often counted from when you are taken to have received the notice, not from when you opened the email.
Most cases move through the stages below. You may not need every stage, and a later stage does not pause an earlier deadline.

items.x: **Read the decision letter.** It names the decision, the reasons and any review rights. [Visa refusal](/appeals/visa-refusal) and [visa cancellation](/appeals/visa-cancellation) explain what those letters mean.
**Merits review at the ART.** Where the law allows it, the Administrative Review Tribunal looks at the decision again on the merits. See [ART appeals](/appeals/art-appeals).

**Court review.** If you lose at the ART and believe the law was applied wrongly, a court can look at legal error. It does not rehear the facts. See [Federal Court appeals](/appeals/federal-court-appeals).

**Ministerial Intervention.** This is a request to the Minister after other review options have ended. It is not a further appeal, and there is no right to a particular outcome. See [Ministerial Intervention](/appeals/ministerial-intervention).

**A notice before cancellation.** If you hold a notice of intention to consider cancellation, the date to reply is in that notice. See [notice of intention to consider cancellation](/appeals/notice-of-intention-to-consider-cancellation).

blocks.label: Note
blocks.x: General information only. It is not legal advice for your situation. The ART, the Department of Home Affairs, the Minister and the courts decide outcomes.

blocks.x: People use the word appeal for three things that do not work the same way. Picking the wrong one wastes the deadline on the right one.

seo.title: Australian Visa Refusal Guide | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: What to do after an Australian visa refusal: ART review deadlines, the AUD 3,727 fee, and when you can apply again.

intro: Visa refusal occurs when an application for an Australian visa is declined by the Department of Home Affairs or a review tribunal. If your visa application is refused, you may have options to seek a review or appeal depending on the type of visa and grounds for refusal.

blocks.x: What is a visa refusal?

A visa refusal means your application for a visa to enter or remain in Australia has been declined. This decision can be made by the Department of Home Affairs or by a merits review tribunal such as the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART). Common reasons for refusal include not meeting health, character, or eligibility requirements.
Types of visa refusals

Visa refusals can relate to various visa categories, including migration visas, protection (refugee) visas, student visas, and visitor visas. Refusals may be based on factors such as incomplete applications, failure to satisfy criteria, or adverse information about the applicant.
What happens after a visa refusal?

If your visa is refused, you will receive a written notice explaining the reasons for refusal and your rights to seek a review or appeal. The options available depend on the visa type and the grounds for refusal.
Seeking a merits review

For many visa refusals, you can apply for a merits review by the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART). The ART reviews the decision afresh and can affirm, vary, or set aside the original decision. Read the deadline in the refusal letter. For most refusals it is 28 days after notification, or 14 days if you are in immigration detention. The fee for most migration reviews is AUD 3,727 and must be paid before that deadline.
Appealing to the courts

If you believe the tribunal or decision-maker made a legal error, you may be able to appeal to the Federal Circuit or Federal Court of Australia. Appeals focus on legal errors rather than re-examining facts or evidence.
Ministerial Intervention

In some cases, if all review and appeal options are exhausted or unavailable, you may request Ministerial Intervention under sections 351 or 501J of the Migration Act. This is a discretionary power where the Minister may grant a visa despite refusal decisions, but it is not guaranteed and subject to strict criteria.
Important considerations

items.x: Pay attention to deadlines for review or appeal applications.
Provide all required documents and evidence to support your case.
Understand that visa refusal can affect your ability to remain in or return to Australia.

blocks.x: Review deadlines

The time limit is in your Department of Home Affairs decision letter. For most visa refusals reviewed by the Administrative Review Tribunal, you have 28 days after you are notified of the decision. If you are in immigration detention when you are notified, the limit is 14 days. A character decision made by a delegate, when you are in Australia, is usually 9 days. The Tribunal cannot extend the 28-day or 14-day limit. A late application is not a valid application.
ART application fee

The fee for a review of most migration decisions under Part 5 of the Migration Act is AUD 3,727. You must pay it before the deadline. In cases of financial hardship the Tribunal may reduce it by 50 percent, and you still have to pay at least half before the deadline. A bridging visa decision that resulted in immigration detention has no fee. A character-related review uses a different fee, currently AUD 1,195. Check the [ART fees page](https://www.art.gov.au/help-and-resources/fees) before you lodge. Figures checked November 2026.

sections.name: What the letter allows
sections.h2: A refusal letter is a set of options, not a single appeal

blocks.x: A refusal means that application was not granted. It is not the same as a cancellation of a visa you already hold. The letter tells you whether you can ask the Administrative Review Tribunal to look at the decision again, whether the decision can only be challenged in court for a legal error, or whether there is no review. Those are different products with different deadlines.

For many visa refusals made while you are in Australia, you can apply to the ART for a merits review. The Tribunal can look at the facts again and can affirm the refusal, remit it to the Department, or set it aside. It cannot invent a visa you were never eligible for. If you were outside Australia when you applied, many refusals have no ART review. Do not pay a review fee until we have read the letter.

items.x: **Find the deemed receipt date.** Time often runs from when you were taken to have received the letter, which can be before you opened the email.
**Many ART review applications must be lodged within 21 or 28 days.** The number is in your letter. It is not the same for every visa, and it is shorter for some detention decisions.
**The review fee has to be paid by the deadline** unless a fee reduction is granted. A form without the fee can be invalid.
**A new visa application is sometimes a better path than a review,** and sometimes it is blocked by section 48, condition 8503, or a re-entry ban. We compare the two before you choose.

sections.h2: How we help with a refusal

blocks.x: A registered migration agent reads the decision record, not only the cover page. The record shows which criterion failed. A review that repeats the original documents, without answering that criterion, is how people lose twice.

items.x: We tell you, in the first call, whether a review appears open and when it must be lodged.
We separate a weak case from a case that failed on a missing document. Only the second is a good candidate for a fast remittal.

We prepare the review application and the submissions. If the issue is a legal error and merits review is finished or unavailable, we say so and refer you to a lawyer for court. Agents do not run Federal Court cases.
We look at whether you can stay lawfully on a bridging visa while a review is pending, and what work condition that bridging visa has.

faqs.a: No. It depends on the visa, where you were, and who made the decision. The letter is the source. Some refusals can only go to court, and some cannot be reviewed at all.

faqs.q: How long do I have?
faqs.a: The limit is in the letter. For many migration decisions it is 21 or 28 days from deemed notification. Do not count from the day you noticed the email.

faqs.q: Can I apply for another visa instead?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If you are in Australia and do not hold a substantive visa, section 48 can limit you to a short list of visas. Condition 8503 can block a further application even if you are still lawful.

faqs.q: Do you go to the Federal Court?
faqs.a: No. Court work is done by a lawyer. We help you see whether the problem is a legal error worth briefing.

seo.title: Australian Visa Cancellation Guide | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Visa cancellation occurs when the Australian Department of Home Affairs or a review tribunal decides to cancel an existing visa, which may require the.

intro: Visa cancellation occurs when the Australian Department of Home Affairs or a review tribunal decides to cancel an existing visa, which may require the visa holder to leave Australia. Cancellation can happen for various reasons including character concerns, breach of visa conditions, or other statutory grounds.

blocks.x: What is visa cancellation?

Visa cancellation is the formal revocation of a visa that has already been granted. This means the visa holder’s permission to stay in Australia is withdrawn, often resulting in the requirement to depart the country. Cancellation decisions can be made by the Department of Home Affairs or by a merits review tribunal such as the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART).
Common reasons for visa cancellation

Visas may be cancelled for reasons including but not limited to: failing to meet character requirements (such as criminal convictions), providing false or misleading information, breaching visa conditions, or involvement in activities that pose a risk to the Australian community.
Notification and rights

If your visa is cancelled, you will receive a written notice explaining the reasons and your rights to seek a review or appeal. You may have limited time to apply for a merits review or appeal depending on the circumstances and visa type.
Seeking a merits review

You can often apply for a merits review of a visa cancellation decision with the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART). The ART will reconsider the decision and can affirm, vary, or set aside the cancellation based on the merits of your case.
Appealing to the courts

If you believe the tribunal or decision-maker made a legal error in cancelling your visa, you may be able to appeal to the Federal Circuit or Federal Court of Australia. Appeals focus on legal errors rather than re-examining facts or evidence.
Ministerial Intervention

If all review and appeal options are exhausted or unavailable, you may request Ministerial Intervention under sections 351 or 501J of the Migration Act. This discretionary power allows the Minister to grant a visa despite cancellation decisions, but it is subject to strict criteria and is not guaranteed.
Getting help
It is strongly recommended to seek legal advice or assistance from registered migration agents or community legal services to understand your options and prepare your case effectively.
Important considerations

items.x: Pay close attention to deadlines for review or appeal applications.
Provide all relevant documents and evidence to support your case.
Visa cancellation can have serious consequences, including detention and removal from Australia.

blocks.x: Cancellation takes away a visa you already hold. The power used in the notice decides what you can argue and where you can go next.

items.x: **Section 116.** A general power. Common reasons include a breach of a condition (for example 8607 on a Skills in Demand visa, 8202 on a student visa, or 8101 work when work was not allowed), a change in circumstances, or the visa having been granted on wrong information.

**Incorrect information.** A visa can be cancelled because false or misleading information was given, even if the rest of your stay has been lawful. The answer is to correct the record, not to ignore the notice.

**Section 501 character.** A different, heavier process. It can lead to detention and removal. Some character decisions are made by a delegate and some by the Minister personally. A personal ministerial decision is often not reviewable at the ART.
**Student-specific and visitor-specific powers** also exist. Read the section number on the first page of the notice before you read anyone's generic advice.

blocks.x: If you have a notice of intention and no decision yet, you are not cancelled. Go to the [NOICC page](/appeals/notice-of-intention-to-consider-cancellation). The response window is the best chance you have.

sections.name: After cancellation
sections.h2: What happens after the visa is cancelled

blocks.x: You may become unlawful the moment the cancellation takes effect, unless a bridging visa is granted or you already hold another visa. Detention is possible if you are unlawful. Do not book a flight, start a new job, or leave Australia until you know whether you still have a visa and whether leaving ends your review.

Merits review, where it exists, can be as short as a few days for a person in detention and longer for a person in the community. The date is in the decision. A review does not automatically give you work rights. Ask what bridging visa you hold and whether it carries condition 8101.
A lawyer, not a migration agent, runs any later case in the Federal Court. We will tell you if we think the Tribunal or the Department made a legal error worth briefing.

sections.name: How we help
sections.h2: How we help with a cancellation

items.x: We identify the section and the deadline on the day you call.
We draft the response if you are still at the notice stage, or the review if a decision has been made.
We collect the evidence that matches the ground: enrolment and attendance for an 8202 breach, employer records for an 8607 breach, or a full account of the information that was wrong.
We tell you plainly if the prospects are poor. A review fee spent on a case with no argument is not a strategy.

faqs.q: I breached a condition once. Will the visa be cancelled?
faqs.a: Not always. Some powers are discretionary. The Department looks at the breach and at the hardship. A notice is your chance to put that hardship on the file. Do not wait for the cancellation to explain it.

faqs.q: Can I work after a cancellation?
faqs.a: Only if you hold a visa that allows work. A bridging visa granted after cancellation often has condition 8101. Working in breach of it is a new problem.

faqs.q: Is a section 501 cancellation reviewable?
faqs.a: Sometimes, if a delegate made it. If the Minister made it personally, merits review is often unavailable. The letter states which one you have.

faqs.q: Can I just leave Australia?
faqs.a: You can, but get advice first. Leaving can change your detention position, your review rights and any ban on return.
