seo.title: Trades Recognition Australia | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Trades Recognition Australia (TRA) provides skills assessments for people with trade or associate‑professional skills gained in Australia or overseas who.

intro: Trades Recognition Australia (TRA) provides skills assessments for people with trade or associate‑professional skills gained in Australia or overseas who intend to migrate or obtain occupational recognition in Australia.

blocks.x: **What TRA does**

Trades Recognition Australia assesses whether your trade or technical skills meet Australian standards for migration and licensing. TRA offers several programs, including the Provisional Skills Assessment, Job Ready Program, Migration Skills Assessment, Offshore Skills Assessment Program, a skills assessment for the Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482), and Migration Points Advice. Home Affairs uses these outcomes.
**Choosing the right program**

Which TRA program applies depends on your occupation, where you studied, your passport country, and the visa you want. The Job Ready Program is for eligible international graduates with an Australian trade or associate qualification. The Offshore Skills Assessment Program is for people outside Australia who need a migration skills assessment. TRA also assesses skills for a Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482) when that visa needs a skills assessment.
**Key assessment programs (brief)**

items.x: Provisional Skills Assessment (PSA): A preliminary step required before entering the Job Ready Program for some international graduates.
Job Ready Program (JRP): A supervised program for eligible international trade graduates in Australia to demonstrate competence and employment readiness.
Migration Skills Assessment (MSA): For applicants seeking permanent skilled migration—evaluates skills against occupational standards for migration purposes.
Offshore Skills Assessment Program (OSAP): For applicants offshore seeking a skills assessment for migration or recognition.
Skills in Demand skills assessment: TRA still labels one program the TSS Skills Assessment. It is the assessment used when a Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482) needs a skills assessment.
Migration Points Advice (MPA): Provides an assessment of how many migration points a particular qualification may attract (where requested by Home Affairs).

blocks.x: **What TRA assesses**

TRA assessments consider the relevant Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) level for the occupation and evidence of competency in practical skills and knowledge. Assessments commonly include review of qualifications, employment history, job duties, and any required licensing information. TRA may reference the Australian Qualifications by Occupation guidance to determine the expected AQF level.
**Documents and evidence you need**

Prepare certified copies (and accredited English translations where applicable) of: passport/ID, qualifications and academic transcripts, detailed employment references describing duties and hours, evidence of registration or licensing (if applicable), and any other program‑specific forms. TRA publishes program‑specific evidence requirements and forms—check the relevant guidelines before applying.
**How to apply (overview)**

items.x: Use the TRA Program Pathfinder to identify the correct program for your circumstances.
Check the Australian Qualifications by Occupation to confirm required AQF level.
Prepare and certify all required documents and complete any program‑specific forms (e.g., PSA or JRP forms).
Lodge your application through TRA’s online portal and pay the applicable fee.
Respond promptly to any TRA requests for further information or verifications.

blocks.x: **Processing, outcomes and review**

Processing times vary by program and application completeness. TRA issues an outcome (suitable / not suitable / provisional) and provides details of any further steps (e.g., required JRP participation or evidence gaps). TRA has an Assessment Review Policy — if you disagree with an outcome you can apply for review under the published procedures and timeframes.
**Licensing and employment**

Some occupations assessed by TRA also require state/territory licensing or registration to work in Australia (e.g., certain construction trades). A positive TRA outcome is an assessment of skills; you must check and meet any separate licensing or regulatory requirements for the occupation and jurisdiction where you plan to work.
**Practical tips and important notes**

items.x: Use TRA’s RTO Finder if you need to locate a Registered Training Organisation for bridging or training.
Remove personal identifiers (e.g., tax file numbers) from documents where advised.
Keep certified originals and scanned copies; ensure translations are by an accredited translator.
Engage a registered migration agent only if you need migration advice—TRA and Home Affairs do not provide personalised migration counselling.

seo.title: Skills Assessment for Trades | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Skills assessment for trades verifies that your overseas or Australian trade qualifications and practical experience meet Australian occupational.

intro: Skills assessment for trades verifies that your overseas or Australian trade qualifications and practical experience meet Australian occupational standards for migration, licensing or employment. Trades Recognition Australia (TRA) runs the main assessment programs and issues outcomes used by the Department of Home Affairs and state/territory licensing bodies.

blocks.x: **Which applicants need a trade skills assessment**
If you have trade or associate‑professional skills (construction, electrical, plumbing, automotive, cook, welder, etc.) and you want to:

items.x: apply for skilled migration to Australia, or
satisfy employer / visa requirements (e.g., TSS 482), or
obtain occupational recognition or licensing in Australia, then you will usually need a TRA skills assessment (or the relevant assessing authority specified for your occupation).

blocks.x: **TRA programs (choose by occupation, visa type, location)**

items.x: Provisional Skills Assessment (PSA) — preliminary step for some international graduates before entering the Job Ready Program.
Job Ready Program (JRP) — for eligible international graduates with an Australian trade/associate qualification to demonstrate competence through employment and monitored milestones.
Migration Skills Assessment (MSA) — for applicants seeking permanent migration; assesses skills against Australian occupational standards.
Offshore Skills Assessment Program (OSAP) — for applicants outside Australia seeking a migration skills assessment.
Skills in Demand skills assessment — TRA still calls this the TSS Skills Assessment. It is for a subclass 482 application that needs a skills assessment.
Migration Points Advice (MPA) — optional advice to Home Affairs on how many migration points a qualification may attract.

blocks.x: Use the TRA Program Pathfinder to select the correct program for your circumstances.
**What TRA assesses**

items.x: Qualification level (AQF equivalence) for your occupation.
Practical competency: duties, experience, hours worked, and demonstrable trade skills.
Evidence of any required licensing or registration.
Program‑specific requirements (e.g., JRP employment milestones).

blocks.x: TRA compares your documentation and experience to Australian occupational criteria and either issues a suitable outcome, a provisional outcome with conditions (e.g., complete JRP), or not suitable.
**Documents typically required**

items.x: Passport biographical page / ID.
Certified copies of trade qualification(s) and full academic transcripts.
Detailed employment references that specify duties, start/end dates, hours per week and employer contact details.
Evidence of licensing or registration if applicable.
Program‑specific forms (PSA/JRP forms) and any supporting evidence.
Accredited English translations for non‑English documents.

blocks.x: Always check the specific evidence checklist in the TRA program guidelines for your occupation.
**How to apply (overview)**

items.x: Use TRA’s Program Pathfinder and Australian Qualifications by Occupation to confirm program/AQF level.
Prepare and certify all required documents; get translations if needed.
Create an account and lodge your application via the TRA online portal; pay the fee.
Respond promptly to requests for additional information or verifications.
Receive TRA outcome and follow any further steps (e.g., JRP enrolment, RTO training, licensing applications).

blocks.x: **Outcomes, validity and review**

items.x: Outcomes may be “suitable”, “provisional” (requires further steps) or “not suitable”.
Processing times and validity periods vary by program and completeness of documents.
TRA publishes an Assessment Review Policy — if you disagree with an outcome you can apply for review within the published timeframe.

blocks.x: **Licensing and employment next steps**

items.x: Some trades also require state/territory licensing (e.g., electrical, gasfitting, building). A positive TRA outcome does not automatically grant a licence — contact the relevant regulator.
Use TRA’s RTO Finder if you need bridging training or to meet licensing requirements.

blocks.x: **Practical tips**

items.x: Remove sensitive identifiers (e.g., tax file numbers) from supporting documents if advised.
Ensure employment references clearly describe actual tasks and hours — generic references may delay assessment.
Keep certified originals and digital copies; follow TRA’s certification and translation rules exactly.
If unsure about visa strategy, consult the Department of Home Affairs or a registered migration agent (TRA does not provide migration advice).

blocks.x: **Where to get help**

items.x: Start with the TRA Program Pathfinder, the program guidelines and FAQs on the TRA website.
For visa matters contact the Department of Home Affairs. For licensing contact the relevant state/territory regulator.
Consider a registered migration agent or approved RTO if you need help with complex cases or bridging training.

seo.description: The Job Ready Program (JRP) is an employment‑based skills assessment run by Trades Recognition Australia (TRA) for eligible international graduates with.

intro: The Job Ready Program (JRP) is an employment‑based skills assessment run by Trades Recognition Australia (TRA) for eligible international graduates with an Australian trade or associate‑degree qualification. The JRP helps you develop workplace skills in Australia and produces a skills‑assessment outcome that can be used when applying for a skilled migration visa.

blocks.x: What the Job Ready Program is

The JRP is an on‑the‑job pathway that lets eligible international graduates demonstrate they meet Australian occupational standards through supervised employment and milestone checks. It is available only after a successful Provisional Skills Assessment (PSA) that verifies your Australian qualification and identifies you as eligible to enter the JRP.
Who the JRP is for
The JRP is for international students who:

items.x: hold an Australian trade or associate professional qualification issued by a Registered Training Organisation (RTO), and
have completed a Provisional Skills Assessment confirming their qualification is suitable for the JRP, and
meet any program and visa eligibility requirements (for example, lawful onshore status and appropriate work rights).

blocks.x: Check your PSA outcome and TRA guidance to confirm eligibility before applying.
Program structure and key steps

items.x: Complete a Provisional Skills Assessment (PSA) and receive a PSA outcome that allows JRP entry.
Enrol in the JRP through TRA’s online portal and pay the program fee.
Undertake employment in your nominated occupation in Australia and meet the JRP milestones (periods of assessed employment, evidence submissions and workplace‑based verification).
TRA reviews submitted employment evidence and may require workplace assessments or RTO involvement where specified.
On successful completion of JRP requirements, TRA issues a final Migration Skills Assessment outcome suitable for Home Affairs visa applications.

blocks.x: TRA may refer to program components/forms such as JRE/JRWA/JRFA — consult TRA guidance for what applies to your occupation.
What TRA assesses in the JRP
TRA assesses:

items.x: whether your practical workplace performance meets Australian occupational standards;
employment evidence (duties, hours, period of work, employer contacts);
any program‑specific competency demonstrations or workplace assessments required for your trade.

blocks.x: A successful JRP outcome confirms you have the trade skills required for migration and employment in Australia.
Documents and evidence you will need
Typical documents include:

items.x: PSA outcome and RTO qualification paperwork;
passport/identity documents;
employment contracts, payslips and detailed employer references (duties, dates, hours);
any workplace assessment reports or RTO certificates requested by TRA;
accredited English translations for non‑English documents where required.

blocks.x: Follow TRA’s program‑specific evidence checklist exactly to avoid delays.
Timeframes and fees

items.x: The JRP requires a minimum participation period (TRA publishes the exact minimum, commonly 12 months for many streams).
Processing times vary depending on completeness of evidence and program workload.
Fees apply for PSA, JRP enrolment and any workplace assessment components — check TRA for current fees and published processing times.

blocks.x: Outcomes and next steps

items.x: Outcomes can be “suitable” (successful skills assessment), “provisional” (further steps required) or “not suitable.”
A successful JRP outcome is used when lodging skilled migration applications with the Department of Home Affairs.
A positive TRA outcome does not replace any state/territory licensing or registration requirements — check licensing rules for your occupation and jurisdiction.

blocks.x: Appeals and reviews
If you disagree with a TRA decision, TRA publishes an Assessment Review Policy and procedures for requesting a review. Follow the specified timeframes and instructions exactly.
Practical tips

items.x: Begin with the TRA Program Pathfinder to confirm the correct program for your situation.
Prepare employer references that clearly describe actual tasks, hours and supervision — vague references can delay assessment.
Keep certified copies and originals of all documents; ensure translations are by accredited translators.
Track your application in the TRA online portal and respond promptly to any requests for additional evidence.

seo.description: A practical checklist before you pay an assessing authority: occupation choice, documents, employment references and what causes a negative outcome.
seo.h1: Skills Assessment Guide for Australian Immigration

hero.h1: Skills Assessment Guide for Australian Immigration
intro: Use this page to prepare the file. The overview of authorities, occupations and fees now sits on the [skills assessment hub](/skill-assessment). This page is the checklist we use before an application is paid.

sections.name: Before you pay
sections.h2: Decide the occupation before you pay the fee

blocks.x: The occupation you nominate has to match both your evidence and the visa you want. An assessing authority will not pick a more convenient occupation for you after you lodge. Changing occupation later usually means a new fee.

items.x: **Read the authority's occupation definition,** not only the job title you use at work. "Manager" and "specialist" are assessed differently.

**Check which visas that occupation opens.** Some occupations are on a skilled list but not on the list your state nominates. Some need a different authority, such as [ACS](/skill-assessment/acs-skill-assessment), [Engineers Australia](/skill-assessment/ea-skill-assessment) or [VETASSESS](/skill-assessment/vetassess-skill-assessment).

**Check the points you can actually prove.** A skills assessment and the points test are related, but a positive assessment does not award points by itself. Use the [points calculator](/migrate-to-australia/pr-point-calculator) only with evidence you already have.

**Trades are a different path.** Many trades go to [Trades Recognition Australia](/skill-assessment/trades-recognition-australia) or the [Job Ready Program](/skill-assessment/job-ready-program), not to a general professional assessor.

sections.name: Documents
sections.h2: Documents to collect before you start the form

items.x: Passport bio page and evidence of any name change.
Degree or trade certificate, full transcript, and a NAATI translation if the original is not in English. A completion letter is not a substitute for the parchment if the authority asks for the award.
Employment references on letterhead that state the job title, exact dates, hours per week, and duties. Generic references that say "various duties" are a common reason for a negative result.
Pay evidence, tax records or social security records that match the dates in the reference. A reference the payment records do not support is worse than a gap you explain.
A résumé that uses the same dates and titles as the references. Do not keep two versions.
Proof of registration or a licence, if the occupation needs one. Nurses, teachers, doctors and some trades are in this group.

blocks.x: Organise the file in the order the authority's checklist uses. Uploading a single unsorted PDF makes it harder for the assessor to find the dates they need, and it slows the review.

sections.name: Negative outcomes
sections.h2: Why skills assessments come back negative

items.x: **The qualification is below the level** the occupation requires, or it is in a field the authority will not accept as closely related.
**The work was not paid, not at least 20 hours a week, or not after the qualification,** where the authority has that rule.
**Duties do not match the occupation.** A job title that sounds right, with duties that belong to a different code, is assessed on the duties.
**Dates conflict** between the résumé, the reference and the tax records.
**The wrong authority.** An ICT applicant at VETASSESS, or a general professional at ACS, loses the fee.

blocks.x: A negative result is not a Department refusal, but you will have to declare problems honestly in later visa forms if you describe your history differently. If you already have a negative outcome, bring the decision record. A review, if the authority offers one, has its own deadline and fee.
Processing times and fee ranges change. Use the [timeline page](/skill-assessment/timeline) and the [requirements page](/skill-assessment/requirements), then confirm both on the authority's own site.

seo.description: Complete guide to skills assessment requirements for all major Australian assessing authorities. Learn about document requirements, qualifications, work experience, and eligibility criteria for ACS, VETASSESS, Engineers Australia, TRA, ANMAC, and more.

intro: Detailed requirements for skills assessment applications across all major assessing authorities in Australia. Compare document requirements, qualifications, work experience, and English language criteria.

blocks.x: Skills Assessment Requirements by Authority

Understanding the specific requirements for your skills assessment is crucial for a successful application. This comprehensive guide breaks down the requirements for all major assessing authorities in Australia, helping you prepare a complete and compelling application.
ACS (Australian Computer Society) Requirements

items.x: **ICT Major:** Bachelor or higher in ICT - Requires 2 years relevant work experience
**ICT Minor:** Bachelor with ICT minor - Requires 4 years relevant work experience
**Non-ICT Qualification:** Bachelor in non-ICT field - Requires 6 years relevant work experience
**No Tertiary:** Vendor certifications + 6 years experience may be considered
Detailed employment references on company letterhead
Must specify job title, dates, duties, and hours per week
Supervisor name, title, and contact details required

seo.title: Citizenship by Conferral | Australian Citizenship | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Becoming an Australian citizen by conferral is a common pathway for permanent residents and New Zealand Special Category visa (SCV) holders who meet.

intro: Becoming an Australian citizen by conferral is a common pathway for permanent residents and New Zealand Special Category visa (SCV) holders who meet eligibility criteria. This process involves applying for citizenship, meeting residency and character requirements, and intending to live in or maintain a connection with Australia.

blocks.x: **Overview of citizenship by conferral**

Citizenship by conferral is available to permanent residents, including New Zealand citizens holding a Special Category (subclass 444) visa, who meet specific criteria. Applicants must be in Australia when their application is decided in most cases and intend to live in Australia or maintain a lasting link if living overseas.
**Eligibility requirements**

items.x: You must be a permanent resident or a New Zealand SCV holder at the time of application and decision.
You generally need to have lived in Australia for a specified period and meet character requirements.
Applicants aged 59 years or under follow the standard process; different provisions apply for those aged 60 or over, or with certain impairments.
New Zealand SCV holders are considered permanent residents for citizenship purposes.
Changes to permanent residency commencement dates may affect eligibility for some New Zealand SCV holders or subclass 189 visa holders.

blocks.x: **Application details**

items.x: A parent can include a dependent child aged 15 years or younger on their application at no extra cost, provided the child is a permanent resident.
Children aged 16 or 17 must apply separately.
There is no application fee for children 15 years or younger applying with a responsible parent.
Fee concessions and exemptions may apply in certain circumstances.

blocks.x: **After you apply**
You can check processing times on the Department of Home Affairs website. The Department will assess your application, including residency, character, and other eligibility criteria.
**Additional notes**

items.x: Some people may already be Australian citizens by birth or descent and may be eligible for an Evidence of Australian Citizenship instead of applying for conferral.
Special pathways exist for people aged 60 or over, those with impairments, or other specific circumstances.

blocks.x: **Fees**
For detailed citizenship fees, refer to Form 1298i – Citizenship application fees.

sections.name: Common refusal reasons
sections.h2: Common reasons these applications are refused

blocks.x: Citizenship by conferral is refused when residence, identity, character or the test is not met.

items.x: **You were outside Australia** too much in the four-year and one-year residence periods.
**You were not a permanent resident** for the required time, including time on a temporary or bridging visa that does not count.
**Identity documents** do not connect your names.
**Character,** including domestic violence orders or a sentence of imprisonment.
**The citizenship test** is not passed, or you do not attend the interview.

blocks.x: A refusal stays on your record. If you already have a refusal letter, read [visa refusal](/appeals/visa-refusal) and check the deadline before you reapply.
Citizenship is not a visa. Visa conditions such as 8607 and 8503 stop applying once you are a citizen, but they still apply to any visa you hold until the pledge.

items.x: **You must hold a visa** that keeps you lawful until the ceremony. Permanent residence travel facilities still matter if you travel before the pledge.
**The residence calculator** is unforgiving of long trips. Count days before you apply.
**A refused citizenship application** does not cancel your permanent visa by itself.
**Children included** in a parent's application have their own identity rules.

blocks.x: The numbers on your grant letter control what you can do. If a condition is breached, the visa can be cancelled. See [visa cancellation](/appeals/visa-cancellation) and, if you have a notice, [notice of intention to consider cancellation](/appeals/notice-of-intention-to-consider-cancellation).

seo.title: Citizenship By Descent | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Australian citizenship by descent is available to individuals born outside Australia who have at least one parent who was an Australian citizen at the.

intro: Australian citizenship by descent is available to individuals born outside Australia who have at least one parent who was an Australian citizen at the time of their birth. This pathway allows eligible applicants to claim citizenship based on their parentage.

blocks.x: **Overview of citizenship by descent**

If you were born overseas and one or both of your parents were Australian citizens when you were born, you may be eligible to apply for Australian citizenship by descent. This process confirms your citizenship status based on your parent’s citizenship and grants you the same rights and responsibilities as other Australian citizens.
**Eligibility requirements**
To be eligible for citizenship by descent, you must:

items.x: Have been born outside Australia.
Have at least one parent who was an Australian citizen at the time of your birth.
Be of good character if you are 18 years or older when applying.
Provide sufficient evidence to prove your parentage and your parent’s citizenship status at the time of your birth.

blocks.x: **Important notes**

items.x: If you are already an Australian citizen and need proof, you can apply for Evidence of Australian citizenship instead.
Applicants aged 15 years or younger must have their application signed by a parent or legal guardian.
A bridging visa cannot be granted while your citizenship by descent application is being processed, so you must ensure you have valid visa status if you are in Australia.
The application fee applies, with reduced fees available for siblings applying together at the same time.

blocks.x: **Application process**

The application requires submitting a completed form along with supporting documents such as your birth certificate, your parent’s proof of Australian citizenship, and identity documents. The Department of Home Affairs will assess your application and may request additional information if needed.
**Processing times**

Processing times can vary depending on the volume of applications and the completeness of your submission. It is recommended to check the Department’s website for current processing times and to apply well in advance if you need citizenship for travel or other purposes.
**Rights and responsibilities**

Once granted citizenship by descent, you will have the same rights as other Australian citizens, including the right to live, work, and vote in Australia, as well as access to Australian passports and consular assistance overseas.

sections.name: Common refusal reasons
sections.h2: Common reasons these applications are refused

blocks.x: Citizenship by descent is refused when a parent was not an Australian citizen at the time of your birth, or the documents do not prove it.

items.x: **The parent became a citizen after you were born.**
**The parent was a permanent resident, not a citizen.**
**Birth and parent documents** do not match, or a name change is undocumented.
**The application is under the wrong provision** for a child born in Australia. That can be citizenship by birth, not descent.

blocks.x: A refusal stays on your record. If you already have a refusal letter, read [visa refusal](/appeals/visa-refusal) and check the deadline before you reapply.
Descent is a citizenship application, not a visa. If you are outside Australia you may still need a visa or a citizenship certificate before you travel.

items.x: **A citizenship certificate is not a visa label.** Airlines may still need the certificate details.
**Condition 8503** on a current visa is irrelevant to the citizenship test, but it still stops other visa applications.
**False documents** in a descent application are a character problem for life.
See [citizenship by birth](/citizenship/citizenship-by-birth) if the child was born in Australia.

blocks.x: The numbers on your grant letter control what you can do. If a condition is breached, the visa can be cancelled. See [visa cancellation](/appeals/visa-cancellation) and, if you have a notice, [notice of intention to consider cancellation](/appeals/notice-of-intention-to-consider-cancellation).

seo.title: Citizenship by Birth in Australia | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Find out if a child born in Australia is a citizen, how the 10-year rule works, and what papers you need.

intro: A baby born in Australia is not always an Australian citizen. From 20 August 1986, being born here is not enough on its own.

Your child is a citizen if one parent was an Australian citizen or a permanent resident when they were born. If not, they can become a citizen on their 10th birthday, but only if Australia has been their home for all of those 10 years.

head: Fact
Detail
rows: Born on or after that date
One parent was a citizen or permanent resident, or the 10-year rule applies
Student, visitor, work and bridging visas do not make a child a citizen at birth
None. It happens on its own when the rule is met
Proof of citizenship, or an Australian passport

blocks.x: Citizenship by birth is set out in section 12 of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007. There are two ways it can happen. You do not fill in a form to be given this citizenship. There is no citizenship test and no ceremony.

items.x: **One parent was a citizen or a permanent resident.** Your child is an Australian citizen from the day they are born.
**The 10-year rule.** Your child was not a citizen at birth, and Australia was their home for the whole of the first 10 years. They become a citizen on their 10th birthday.

blocks.x: Most families contact us when they apply for a passport, or when a school, Medicare or an employer asks for proof. Sometimes the child is already a citizen and only needs the right papers. Sometimes they are not a citizen yet, and they need a visa.
A child born overseas to an Australian parent is a different case. That is [citizenship by descent](/citizenship/citizenship-by-descent). You do need to apply for that.

sections.name: Eligibility by date of birth
sections.h2: The date of birth decides the rule

blocks.x: The law changed on 20 August 1986. People born before that date are not in the same position as people born on or after it. They also need different papers.
Born in Australia before 20 August 1986

You are usually an Australian citizen from birth. A full birth certificate from the state or territory registry is normally enough to show this. A pretty certificate from the hospital is not the full birth certificate. Order the official one from the registry of births, deaths and marriages.
There is one main exception. If a parent was a diplomat or a consular officer for another country when you were born, do not assume the birth certificate is enough. Ask us to check.
Born in Australia on or after 20 August 1986

You are a citizen from birth if at least one parent was an Australian citizen or a permanent resident on that day. A permanent resident is someone who held a permanent visa. A student visa, visitor visa, graduate visa, temporary work visa or bridging visa is not a permanent visa.

The birth certificate shows where you were born and who your parents are. For anyone born on or after 20 August 1986, it does not prove citizenship on its own. You also need proof of the parent's status on the day you were born. That can be their citizenship certificate, their own Australian birth certificate if they were born here before 20 August 1986, or their passport and permanent visa.

If a parent died before the birth, the law uses that parent's status on the day they died. If that parent was also born in Australia on or after 20 August 1986, you may need to show that a grandparent was an Australian citizen when the parent was born.

sections.name: Who this is for
sections.h2: Being born here does not give a baby a visa

blocks.x: This is the part that surprises most parents on a temporary visa. The baby is born in Australia. The family thinks the baby is Australian. They only find out the truth when they apply for a passport, or when they try to enrol the child with Medicare as a citizen.

If neither parent was an Australian citizen or a permanent resident, the child is not a citizen at birth. Being born here also does not put the child on a parent's visa. Check the child's visa. Tell Home Affairs about the birth. Apply for a visa for the child if they need one. If you wait until the family's visas run out, the child can be in Australia without a visa.

A birth on Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands or Norfolk Island counts as a birth in Australia. A child born on a ship or plane registered in Australia is also treated as born in Australia. A child born on an unregistered ship or plane that belongs to another country's government is treated as born in that country.

Australian law decides who a parent is. That includes some cases of IVF and surrogacy under the Family Law Act 1975. The names on a birth record from another country are not always the parents Australian law recognises. Get advice before you apply for a passport after surrogacy, or where a donor was involved.

The 10-year rule is for a child born in Australia on or after 20 August 1986 who was not a citizen at birth. If Australia was the child's home for the full 10 years from the day they were born, they become an Australian citizen on their 10th birthday. You do not lodge a form for this to happen.

The law calls this "ordinarily resident". In plain words, Australia has to be the place the child really lives. A short trip away can still count, if Australia stays their home. Time in Australia only for a short or special reason does not count. The child needs a home here for the whole 10 years, not just most of them.

A holiday does not automatically break the 10 years. A long time overseas can. Home Affairs looks at how long each trip was, why the child left, whether the family kept a home in Australia, and whether the parents planned to come back. School reports, Medicare records and proof of address matter. For a child, what the parents did is the evidence.

The visa sticker is not the test. A child can meet the 10-year rule even if they did not hold a visa on every day. A child who only ever held a temporary visa does not meet the rule just because they were allowed to stay. Being in Australia with no visa is still a serious problem. Sort out the child's visa and the citizenship question together.
Papers worth keeping from the start

items.x: The full Australian birth certificate.
Passports, and a list of every trip in and out of Australia, with the reason for each trip.
School, childcare and enrolment letters for the 10 years.
Medicare, immunisation and hospital records.
A lease, bills or other proof the family kept a home in Australia while they were away.

blocks.x: On the 10th birthday, the citizenship is already there if the test is met. You still apply for a citizenship certificate when a school, a passport office or another agency wants a paper that says so. Our page on [evidence of Australian citizenship](/citizenship/evidence-of-australian-citizenship) explains that application.

sections.name: New Zealand citizen parents
sections.h2: If a parent is a New Zealand citizen

blocks.x: New Zealand parents are the case we are asked to check most often. A Special Category visa (subclass 444) does not make the parent a permanent resident for every birth since 1986. It depends on the date of birth, and on the visa the parent held that day. If a parent had diplomatic privileges, these rules usually do not apply.

items.x: **Born before 20 August 1986.** A child born in Australia from 24 November 1952 is usually an Australian citizen. This includes many children of New Zealand citizens.

**20 August 1986 to 31 August 1994.** Many New Zealand citizens in Australia at this time were called exempt non-citizens. A child born here to a parent in that group usually did not become an Australian citizen at birth.
**1 September 1994 to 26 February 2001.** The child is usually a citizen if a parent held a permanent visa or a Special Category visa.

**27 February 2001 to 30 June 2022.** A permanent visa still works. A Special Category visa works only in set cases. One is a parent who was in Australia on that visa on 26 February 2001. Another is a parent who spent at least 12 months on that visa in the two years before that date. A Centrelink letter that says the parent lived in Australia can also be enough.
**On or after 1 July 2022.** A child born in Australia to a parent who held a Special Category visa is usually an Australian citizen by birth.

blocks.x: There is one more tight window. Some children born between 1 January 2022 and 30 June 2023 are citizens if a parent was later granted a New Zealand stream Skilled Independent visa (subclass 189) in that same period. The dates are easy to get wrong. Bring the parent's passport and visa grant letters. We will match them to the day of the birth.

If the child is already a citizen, apply for proof of Australian citizenship. Do not lodge [citizenship by conferral](/citizenship/citizenship-by-conferral) just to find out. Conferral is the application for someone who is not a citizen yet.

sections.name: If the child is not a citizen
sections.h2: If your child is not a citizen yet

blocks.x: You still have a way forward. The right path depends on the child's age, their visa, and whether any other country treats them as a citizen.

items.x: **Get a visa now.** Put the child on a visa. Being born in Australia does not let them stay.
**Wait for the 10th birthday.** If Australia stays their home for the full 10 years, citizenship starts on that day. Keep the school and travel records as you go.

**Apply for citizenship later.** Once the child is a permanent resident, they can apply for citizenship by conferral. A child under 16 can often be added to a parent's application. Conferral has its own rules on time in Australia and character. Most adults also sit the citizenship test and make the pledge.

**A child with no citizenship anywhere.** A person born in Australia who has never been a citizen of any country, and who cannot get one, can apply under the stateless rule in the Act. The Minister decides that application. It does not happen on its own.

blocks.x: A child found abandoned in Australia, where no one can identify the parents, is an Australian citizen unless the opposite is proved. This does not cover a child whose parents are known and hold temporary visas.

sections.name: Documents that prove citizenship
sections.h2: Papers that prove citizenship by birth

blocks.x: Start with a full birth certificate from the registry in the state or territory where the child was born. Then match the other papers to the date of birth.

items.x: **Born before 20 August 1986.** A full Australian birth certificate, a current Australian passport, or an Australian citizenship certificate. One of these is normally enough.

**Born on or after 20 August 1986.** A citizenship certificate or a current Australian passport. If you have neither, give them the full birth certificate plus proof that a parent named on it was an Australian citizen or a permanent resident when you were born.
**The 10-year rule.** The birth certificate, plus school, Medicare, address and travel records that show Australia was the child's home for the whole 10 years.

blocks.x: You apply for the certificate in ImmiAccount. The form is called evidence of Australian citizenship. It is proof of a citizenship the person already has. Home Affairs charges a fee. The current fee is on the [evidence of citizenship page](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/citizenship/certificate).
Australian passports

The Australian Passport Office uses the same date. If you were born in Australia before 20 August 1986, a full birth certificate is usually enough. If you were born on or after that date, they will not treat the birth certificate as proof on its own. You need a citizenship certificate, an older Australian passport that meets their rules, or other proof that a parent was a citizen. Check the list on the [Passport Office citizenship page](https://www.passports.gov.au/citizenship) before you book.

sections.name: After citizenship
sections.h2: What citizenship by birth gives you

blocks.x: A citizen by birth has the same citizenship as someone who became a citizen by application or by descent. They can live and work in Australia with no visa. They can study and use Medicare. They can hold an Australian passport and ask for help from an Australian embassy overseas. From age 18 they must enrol to vote.

Australia has allowed [dual citizenship](/citizenship/dual-citizenship) since 4 April 2002. A child who is Australian by birth may also be a citizen of a parent's country, if that country's law allows it. Some countries give that citizenship automatically. Some do not allow a second citizenship at all. Check that law before you apply for another passport, or before you give a citizenship up. Australian citizenship by birth is not lost because the family lives overseas, or because the child holds another passport.

sections.name: What to bring
sections.h2: What to bring if you want us to check

blocks.x: We can usually tell you, from the date of birth and the parents' visas, whether the child is already a citizen and which form to lodge. Bring what you have. You can order anything that is missing.

items.x: **The child's full birth certificate.** If it has not arrived yet, bring the hospital papers.
**Both parents' passports,** plus any Australian citizenship certificate or permanent visa grant.
**A note of time spent outside Australia,** if the child is close to 10, or is already over 10 and was not a citizen at birth.

blocks.x: Bansal Immigration is in Melbourne. Call +61 3 9602 1330 or book a time to talk. We will tell you whether to apply for proof of citizenship, wait for the 10th birthday, or sort out a visa first.

items.x: [Citizenship by conferral](/citizenship/citizenship-by-conferral). For permanent residents who are not citizens yet, including children born in Australia.
[Citizenship by descent](/citizenship/citizenship-by-descent). For a child born outside Australia to an Australian parent.
[Evidence of Australian citizenship](/citizenship/evidence-of-australian-citizenship). The certificate that proves a citizenship the person already has.
[Australian citizenship test](/citizenship/citizenship-test). For most adults who apply for citizenship. Not for citizenship by birth.
[Dual citizenship](/citizenship/dual-citizenship). Holding Australian citizenship and another citizenship at the same time.

faqs.q: Is every child born in Australia an Australian citizen?
faqs.a: Children born in Australia before 20 August 1986 usually are citizens from birth. Children born on or after that date are citizens at birth only if one parent was an Australian citizen or a permanent resident. If neither parent was, the child becomes a citizen on their 10th birthday only if Australia has been their home for all of those 10 years.

faqs.q: Our baby was born while we were on student visas. Are they a citizen?
faqs.a: Not at birth. A student visa is not permanent residence, and the birth does not give the baby a visa. They need their own visa to stay here lawfully. They can become a citizen at 10 if Australia stays their home for those 10 years. They can also apply later if they become a permanent resident.

faqs.q: Do we lodge a form for citizenship by birth?
faqs.a: No. You do not apply to be given citizenship by birth. It happens on its own when the rule is met. You apply for proof of Australian citizenship when you need a certificate. You apply for citizenship by conferral only if the child is not a citizen yet.

faqs.q: Does a holiday overseas break the 10-year rule?
faqs.a: A short trip does not automatically break it. Australia still has to be the child's home for the whole 10 years. Long trips, or a family that has moved overseas for good, can mean the rule is not met. Keep school, address and travel records for every trip.

faqs.q: Will the birth certificate get my child an Australian passport?
faqs.a: If the child was born in Australia before 20 August 1986, a full birth certificate is usually accepted. If the child was born on or after 20 August 1986, the Passport Office will not treat the birth certificate as proof on its own. You usually need a citizenship certificate, or proof that a parent was an Australian citizen or a permanent resident when the child was born.

faqs.q: We are New Zealand citizens. Is our Australian-born child a citizen?
faqs.a: Sometimes. It depends on the date of birth and the visa you held that day. Children born on or after 1 July 2022 to a parent on a Special Category visa are usually citizens. Many children born between 20 August 1986 and 31 August 1994 to New Zealand parents were not citizens at birth. Bring the parent's passport and we will check the date before you apply.

faqs.q: Can our child be Australian and a citizen of our home country?
faqs.a: Australia allows two citizenships. Your home country might not. Some countries treat the child as their citizen because of the parents. Some ask the child to choose later. The child's Australian citizenship stays either way. Check the other country's law before you apply for a second passport.

hero.h1: Dual Citizenship Australia - Complete Guide to Multiple Citizenships
intro: Australia allows dual or multiple citizenships, enabling Australian citizens to hold citizenship of another country or countries simultaneously. This guide explains the key aspects, benefits, and considerations of holding dual citizenship in Australia.

blocks.x: **What is dual citizenship?**

Dual citizenship means being a citizen of two countries at the same time. Australia permits its citizens to acquire citizenship of another country without losing their Australian citizenship, and vice versa, subject to the laws of the other country.
**Eligibility and acquisition**
You can become a dual citizen by:

items.x: Being born in Australia to parents who are citizens of another country.
Acquiring citizenship of another country through descent, marriage, naturalisation, or other means while retaining Australian citizenship.
Being born overseas to Australian citizen parents and acquiring citizenship of that country as well.

blocks.x: **Benefits of dual citizenship**

items.x: **Travel flexibility:** Hold passports from both countries, easing travel and visa requirements.
**Work and study:** Access to work, study, and social benefits in both countries.
**Voting rights:** Participate in elections in both countries where permitted.
**Consular protection:** Access consular assistance from both countries when abroad.

blocks.x: **Responsibilities and considerations**

items.x: **Legal obligations:** You must comply with the laws of both countries, including taxation and military service where applicable.
**Conflicting laws:** Some countries do not recognize dual citizenship and may require you to renounce other citizenships.
**Security clearances:** Holding dual citizenship can affect eligibility for certain government jobs or security clearances.
**Travel restrictions:** Some countries may restrict entry or impose special conditions on dual citizens.

blocks.x: **How to apply for dual citizenship**

items.x: **Australian citizens acquiring another citizenship:** Generally, you do not need to notify the Australian government but should check the other country’s requirements.
**Foreign nationals applying for Australian citizenship:** You may be required to renounce your previous citizenship depending on your country of origin, though Australia allows dual citizenship.
**Proof of dual citizenship:** You may need to provide evidence of your citizenship status in both countries for legal or administrative purposes.

blocks.x: **Losing Australian citizenship**

Australian citizenship can be lost in rare circumstances, such as fraud in the application process or serving in the armed forces of a country at war with Australia. Simply acquiring another citizenship does not cause loss of Australian citizenship.
**Important advice**

items.x: Check the citizenship laws of the other country involved before applying for or accepting another citizenship.
Seek legal advice if you have concerns about your rights, obligations, or potential conflicts arising from dual citizenship.
Keep documentation of your citizenship status for both countries.

faqs.q: Does Australia allow dual citizenship?
faqs.a: Yes, Australia has allowed dual citizenship since April 4, 2002. You can be an Australian citizen and hold citizenship of one or more other countries at the same time. You do not need to renounce your previous citizenship to become an Australian citizen.

faqs.q: Do I need to renounce my citizenship to become Australian?
faqs.a: No, you do not need to renounce your current citizenship to become an Australian citizen. However, you should check if your current country of citizenship permits dual citizenship, as some countries require you to renounce when acquiring another citizenship.

faqs.q: Will I lose my Australian citizenship if I become a citizen of another country?
faqs.a: No, acquiring citizenship of another country will not automatically affect your Australian citizenship. Australia permits its citizens to hold citizenship of other countries. However, you should check the requirements of the country whose citizenship you are acquiring.

faqs.q: Which passport should I use when traveling?
faqs.a: You must enter and leave Australia on your Australian passport. When entering or leaving your other country of citizenship, you should use that country's passport. For travel to third countries, you can choose which passport to use based on visa requirements and convenience.

faqs.q: Can my children have dual citizenship?
faqs.a: Yes, children can have dual citizenship. This commonly occurs when a child is born in Australia to parents who are citizens of another country, or when born overseas to an Australian parent. The child can maintain both citizenships, subject to the laws of both countries.

faqs.q: What countries don't allow dual citizenship with Australia?
faqs.a: Several countries do not permit dual citizenship, including China (excluding Hong Kong and Macau), Japan, Singapore, Indonesia, India (with some exceptions), and the United Arab Emirates. If you are from one of these countries, you may need to renounce that citizenship to become Australian, or vice versa.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay taxes in both countries as a dual citizen?
faqs.a: Tax obligations depend on the tax laws of each country and your residency status. Generally, Australia taxes residents on worldwide income and non-residents only on Australian-sourced income. You should seek professional tax advice to understand your specific obligations and any tax treaties that may apply.

faqs.q: Can I vote in both countries if I have dual citizenship?
faqs.a: Voting rights depend on the laws of each country. In Australia, citizenship gives you the right (and obligation) to vote in federal and state elections. Your other country of citizenship may also permit or require you to vote. Check the electoral laws of both countries.

faqs.q: Will dual citizenship affect my ability to get security clearance?
faqs.a: Dual citizenship may be considered during security clearance assessments for certain government positions, but it does not automatically disqualify you. Each case is assessed on its individual merits, considering factors such as your ties to the other country and the nature of the position.

faqs.q: Can I serve in the military of another country while holding Australian citizenship?
faqs.a: Generally, serving in the armed forces of a foreign country will not result in automatic loss of Australian citizenship. However, serving in armed forces at war with Australia or engaging in certain security-related activities may have implications. Seek professional advice if considering foreign military service.

faqs.q: How does dual citizenship affect public office eligibility in Australia?
faqs.a: Section 44 of the Australian Constitution prohibits anyone who is a citizen of a foreign power from being a member of federal parliament. State and territory legislatures have similar provisions. If you wish to hold such office, you may need to renounce your other citizenship.

faqs.q: Can I hold dual citizenship if I work for the Australian government?
faqs.a: Yes, many Australian public servants hold dual citizenship. However, some sensitive positions, particularly those requiring high-level security clearances, may have restrictions or additional scrutiny. Requirements vary by agency and position.

Australian Citizenship Test Overview

The Australian Citizenship Test is a mandatory requirement for most people applying for Australian citizenship by conferral. The test assesses your knowledge of Australia, its democratic values, rights and responsibilities of citizenship, and the privileges and responsibilities of being an Australian citizen.

blocks.x: Who Must Take the Test?

faqs.q: How difficult is the Australian citizenship test?
faqs.a: The test is designed to be achievable for anyone who studies the official resource book. With proper preparation, most people pass on their first attempt. The 75% pass mark is reasonable, and all questions come directly from the study materials.

faqs.q: How long should I study for the citizenship test?
faqs.a: Most people spend 2-4 weeks studying the resource book and taking practice tests. The time needed depends on your English proficiency and familiarity with Australian culture and government. We recommend thorough preparation rather than rushing.

faqs.q: What are the Australian values questions?
faqs.a: Australian values questions test your understanding of fundamental principles including: democratic beliefs, freedom and equality, respect for all individuals, rule of law, and parliamentary democracy. You must answer all 5 values questions correctly to pass.

faqs.q: Can I take the test in another language?
faqs.a: No, the citizenship test must be completed in English. However, you can study the resource book in your preferred language first, then practice in English. Preparation materials are available in many languages.

faqs.q: What happens if I fail the citizenship test?
faqs.a: You can retake the test as many times as needed at no additional cost. There is no limit on attempts. You can usually rebook within a few weeks of an unsuccessful attempt. Use the time to study areas you found challenging.

faqs.q: How long does the citizenship test take?
faqs.a: You have 45 minutes to complete the 20 multiple-choice questions. Most people finish in 15-20 minutes. Take your time to read each question carefully and consider your answers.

faqs.q: Where can I take the citizenship test?
faqs.a: Tests are conducted at Department of Home Affairs offices and designated test centers across Australia. Your test invitation will include available locations. Choose the most convenient center when booking.

faqs.q: Can I bring notes or the resource book to the test?
faqs.a: No, the test is closed book. You cannot bring any materials, notes, or electronic devices into the test room. All questions are based on information from the resource book, which you should study beforehand.

seo.description: Evidence of Australian Citizenship is an official document that confirms a person's status as an Australian citizen. It is typically required for various.

intro: Evidence of Australian Citizenship is an official document that confirms a person's status as an Australian citizen. It is typically required for various purposes, such as applying for an Australian passport, enrolling to vote, or proving citizenship to government agencies.

blocks.x: **What is Evidence of Australian Citizenship?**

Evidence of Australian Citizenship is a formal document issued by the Department of Home Affairs that verifies an individual's Australian citizenship status. It serves as official proof of your citizenship, whether you acquired it by birth, descent, or conferral.
**When do you need it?**
You may need Evidence of Australian Citizenship for various reasons, including:

items.x: **Applying for an Australian passport:** This is a primary requirement for first-time passport applicants or those whose previous passport has expired and their citizenship cannot be verified through other means.
**Enrolling to vote:** To register for federal, state, or territory elections.
**Proving citizenship to government agencies:** For employment, social security, or other official purposes.
**Sponsoring family members:** As part of certain visa applications.

**If you were born in Australia:** If you were born in Australia before 20 August 1986, your birth certificate is usually sufficient. If you were born on or after 20 August 1986, you may need to apply for evidence of citizenship if neither of your parents was an Australian citizen or permanent resident at the time of your birth.

blocks.x: **How to apply for Evidence of Australian Citizenship**
You can apply for Evidence of Australian Citizenship through the Department of Home Affairs. The application process typically involves:

items.x: **Completing the application form:** Ensure all sections are filled accurately.

**Providing supporting documents:** This usually includes your birth certificate, identity documents, and documents proving your parents' citizenship or permanent residency status at the time of your birth (if applicable).
**Paying the application fee:** Check the Department's website for current fees.
**Submitting the application:** Lodge your application online via ImmiAccount or by post.

blocks.x: **What documents can serve as evidence?**
While a certificate of Australian citizenship is the most common form of evidence, other documents may also be accepted in specific circumstances, such as:

items.x: An Australian birth certificate (for those born in Australia before 20 August 1986, or born on or after that date to an Australian citizen or permanent resident parent).
A previous Australian passport (if it was issued based on verified citizenship).

blocks.x: **Important considerations**

items.x: Ensure all supporting documents are certified copies.
If any documents are not in English, they must be accompanied by an accredited English translation.
Processing times can vary, so apply well in advance if you need the document for a specific purpose.

blocks.x: By Birth, Descent
You were born in Australia but need to confirm your status, especially if born after 20 August 1986. You became a citizen by descent.

seo.description: A Temporary Resident Visa (TRV) that allows non‑exempt foreign nationals to enter Canada for tourism, visiting family or short business visits for a.

intro: A Temporary Resident Visa (TRV) that allows non‑exempt foreign nationals to enter Canada for tourism, visiting family or short business visits for a limited time.

blocks.x: **Purpose**
Visit Canada for tourism, to see family or friends, or for short‑term business activities (not for local paid employment or long‑term study).
**Who needs a visitor visa**

items.x: Nationals of countries that are not visa‑exempt must apply for a TRV before travelling.
Travellers from visa‑exempt countries who are flying to Canada generally need an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) instead.
Some passport holders may have additional local requirements (e.g., Venezuelan passport holders).

blocks.x: **Who can apply**

People who want to visit Canada temporarily can apply for a visitor visa (TRV) if they are not visa‑exempt; this generally includes applicants who are outside Canada, though in limited circumstances some people already in Canada may also apply. Eligible applicants must genuinely intend a temporary stay, meet identity, health and security requirements (including any requested biometrics, medical exams or police certificates), and be able to demonstrate sufficient funds and ties to return home at the end of their visit.
**Key eligibility points (single-line)**

items.x: Genuine temporary intent to leave Canada at the end of the visit.
Sufficient funds for the stay and return travel.
No criminal inadmissibility or serious health issues.
Meet biometrics, medical exam or other IRCC requests where required.
Provide truthful information and necessary supporting documents.

blocks.x: **How to apply — main steps**

items.x: Determine whether you need a TRV or an eTA.
Create an IRCC online account (or obtain paper forms if eligible).
Complete the application form(s) and the required checklist.
Gather, scan and translate required supporting documents.
Pay the application fee and biometrics fee (if required).
Submit the online application (or mail a paper application).
Provide biometrics at a Visa Application Centre (VAC) or designated location when requested.
Attend medical exams or interviews if IRCC requests them.
Monitor your IRCC account for messages or requests for more information.
If approved, receive the visa vignette in your passport (or eTA electronically) and check the conditions.

blocks.x: **Fees & processing**
Fees vary by country and application type; biometrics and VAC service fees may apply. Processing times change frequently — check IRCC processing times for current estimates and plan accordingly.
**After you apply**

Respond promptly to IRCC requests (biometrics, documents or additional information). Keep copies of what you submitted and do not make travel arrangements that require a visa until you have the required entry authorization.
**Prepare for your arrival**

Carry your passport with the visa/eTA, proof of funds, return ticket and supporting documents. Be ready to explain the purpose and duration of your visit to border services officers and comply with any conditions on the visa.

intro: A visa allowing individuals from non‑visa waiver countries to visit New Zealand for tourism, family visits, or short-term study (up to 3 months), with stays up to 6 or 9 months.

blocks.x: **Purpose**
To visit New Zealand for holidays, to see family and friends, or to study for up to 3 months. This visa does not permit working in New Zealand, except for remote work for an overseas employer.
**Who needs a Visitor Visa**

items.x: People travelling on a passport from countries that are not part of New Zealand's visa waiver program.
Australian citizens travelling on an Australian passport do not need a Visitor Visa or an NZeTA.
Citizens of visa waiver countries or territories can travel with a New Zealand Electronic Travel Authority (NZeTA) instead of a visa.
Specific exceptions exist, such as Chinese and Pacific Islands Forum country citizens travelling from Australia with an eligible Australian visa, who can use an NZeTA.

blocks.x: **Length of stay**

items.x: **Multiple-entry Visitor Visa:** Allows multiple visits, with a maximum stay of 6 months in any 12-month period. To be eligible, you must have been out of New Zealand for at least 9 months in the 18-month period before applying.

**Single-entry Visitor Visa:** Allows one entry and a stay of up to 9 months in an 18-month period. This may be issued if you want to stay longer than 6 months, are extending a current stay, or if a multiple-entry visa is not deemed necessary. If you leave New Zealand on a single-entry visa, it will expire.
**Visitors from the Pacific:** May be eligible for a 24-month multiple-entry Visitor Visa.

blocks.x: **Cost**
From NZD $441 (subject to change).
**Processing time**
80% of applications are processed within 2 weeks.
**Key eligibility points**

items.x: **Good health:** May require a chest X-ray or medical examination, especially if staying over 6 months or from a country with a non-low incidence of tuberculosis.
**Good character:** May require police certificates, particularly if aged 17 or older and your total time in New Zealand will be 24 months or longer.
**Genuine intentions:** Must be a genuine visitor and intend to leave New Zealand at the end of your stay.
**Enough money to live on:** Must have at least NZD $1,000 per month (or NZD $400 if accommodation is pre-paid), or have an acceptable sponsor.
**Ability to leave New Zealand:** Must show proof of a ticket out of New Zealand or sufficient funds to purchase one.

blocks.x: **What this visa lets you do**

items.x: Holiday in New Zealand.
Visit family and friends.
Study for up to 3 months in any 12-month period.
Include your partner and dependent children (aged 19 or younger) in your application.

blocks.x: **When you arrive**

items.x: Complete a New Zealand Traveller Declaration (NZTD).
Be prepared to show a ticket to leave New Zealand or proof of funds for one.
Be prepared to show proof of sufficient funds for your stay.
You can be refused entry if you are not a genuine visitor, do not meet character requirements, or have had a change in circumstances.

blocks.x: **While in New Zealand**

items.x: **Travel:** If you leave New Zealand, your visa will expire unless it has a multiple-entry travel condition.
**Work:** You cannot work, but you may volunteer or work remotely for an overseas employer.
**Study:** You can study for up to 3 months in any 12-month period. School-aged children can study for up to 3 months in any calendar year.

blocks.x: **Staying longer**

If you are in New Zealand and need more time for a genuine reason, you can apply to extend your visit before your current visa expires. A new single-entry Visitor Visa may be granted for up to 9 months in an 18-month period.

seo.h1: Complete Guide to USA Tourist Visa (B-2)

hero.h1: Complete Guide to USA Tourist Visa (B-2)
intro: A nonimmigrant visa for people who want to travel to the United States for short-term business (B-1), tourism or visiting family and friends (B-2), or a combination of both (B-1/B-2).

blocks.x: The B-1/B-2 visitor visa lets foreign nationals enter the U.S. temporarily for business meetings, conferences, tourism, family visits, medical treatment, or short courses of study (if allowed). A visa only lets you travel to a U.S. port of entry U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers decide whether you can enter and for how long.
**Who this visa is for**

items.x: B-1 (Business): people attending meetings, conferences, negotiations, or other short business activities.
B-2 (Tourist): people visiting for holidays, family visits, medical treatment, or short recreational courses.
B-1/B-2 combined: for travellers doing both types of activities.

blocks.x: **Key eligibility points**

items.x: You must have a valid passport.
You must show you intend to stay temporarily and will return home (ties to your country).
You must prove you can pay for your trip or that a sponsor will.
You must meet health and character requirements (police or medical checks may be requested).
You must not intend to work or immigrate while on a visitor visa.

blocks.x: **How to apply (step-by-step)**

items.x: Complete the online DS-160 form and print the confirmation page.
Pay the non‑refundable visa application fee (amount shown on the local U.S. Embassy/Consulate site). The typical fee is USD 185 for most visitor visas.
Schedule a visa interview at the U.S. Embassy or Consulate in your country (appointments vary by location).
Gather required documents (passport, DS-160 confirmation, fee receipt, photo, supporting documents).
Attend the interview and provide fingerprints and any requested documents.
Wait for visa processing or additional administrative processing if required. If approved, pay any issuance fee (if applicable) and arrange passport return.

blocks.x: **Fees & processing times**

items.x: Standard application fee (most nationalities): USD 185
Some nationalities may pay issuance fees after approval.
Interview wait times and processing vary by Embassy/Consulate, season and demand — check local appointment and processing times on your Embassy website.

blocks.x: **Entry, length of stay and extensions**

items.x: A visa does not guarantee entry CBP officers at the port of entry decide admission and length of stay.
If you need to extend your stay or change to another nonimmigrant status while in the U.S., apply to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) before your authorised stay ends.
Overstaying can void your visa and make you ineligible for future visas.

blocks.x: **Tips for a smoother application**

items.x: Be honest and complete on your DS-160 and at your interview.
Carry evidence that shows you will return home (job letter, family, property).
Apply early interview wait times can be long.
Do not make irreversible travel plans (buy non‑refundable tickets) until you have a visa.

seo.description: The Second Post-Higher Education Work stream of the subclass 485 visa is open for eligible regional graduates. The old subclass 476 visa is closed.

intro: This is the Second Post-Higher Education Work stream of the subclass 485 visa. It is a new application, not an extension of your first 485. It is for people whose first 485 came from study at a regional campus, and who then lived in a designated regional area. The old Skilled Recognised Graduate visa (subclass 476) is closed. Do not lodge a 476 application.

head: Fact
Detail
rows: AUD 2,265 for this second stream. A first 485 visa is AUD 5,750
No set time. Check the Department's guide

blocks.x: This is the Second Post-Higher Education Work stream. It is for people who hold a subclass 485 visa in the Post-Higher Education Work stream, or who still hold an older Post-Study Work or Replacement stream visa, after study at an eligible regional institution. The extra stay is 1 or 2 years. It depends on where you studied and where you lived. You must be in Australia to apply, and you must meet the health, character and insurance requirements.

sections.name: Eligibility
sections.h2: Do You Have What It Takes?

items.x: Be 35 or under when you apply. You can be under 50 if you hold a Hong Kong or British National (Overseas) passport, or if a masters by research or a doctoral degree was used to meet the study requirement for your first 485.
Be physically in Australia when you lodge the application
Currently hold a Temporary Graduate (subclass 485) visa in Post Higher Education Work, Post Study Work, or Replacement stream
Have previously held a 485 visa granted in the Post Higher Education Work or Post Study Work stream as the main applicant
Hold a degree from a CRICOS registered course completed at an institution located in an eligible designated regional area that led to your first 485 grant
For at least 2 years immediately before you apply, you lived only in a designated regional area. Any work or study on the first 485 was also only in a designated regional area.
Provide evidence of adequate health insurance for all applicants when applying
Meet health requirements (medical exams may be requested)
Meet character requirements (police certificates may be required)
Continue to satisfy any other departmental requirements for the visa at the time of application
Extend your lawful stay in Australia for an additional 1–2 years

You can work, but condition 8610 means you must live, work and study only in the regional area set when the visa is granted. Use the [Postcode Checker](/postcode-checker) as a guide, then check the Department's regional list.
Study further in Australia during the visa period
Maintain the ability to travel to and from Australia while the visa is valid

From 13 November 2026, a partner or child can be included only in limited cases, and only in the same application as you. They cannot apply later on their own. They usually need to hold a 485 as your dependant now, or to have held one in the last six months, and they must have been on your previous visa. Pacific and ASEAN nationals, people who finished a PhD on a student visa, and people whose course was fully funded by a foreign government can include family who were not on the earlier visa. Read the [Home Affairs family rules](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-listing/changes-to-temporary-graduate-visa-subclass-485-family-member-rules).
Gain additional regional work experience that can strengthen permanent residence prospects
Remain lawfully in Australia while you explore further visa or sponsorship options
Access local employment and community networks in regional areas
Use the extra time to meet requirements for other permanent or employer sponsored visas
Provide continuity of status if your first 485 visa is expiring and you meet extension criteria
Confirm you meet all eligibility criteria, especially the 2 year regional residence rule
Collect proof of your degree from the eligible regional institution that led to your first 485 grant
Gather evidence of continuous residence in the designated regional area for the required 2 years (leases, utility bills, employment records)
Ensure you currently hold the required 485 visa stream and have documentation of that visa grant
Obtain and prepare identity documents (passport, birth certificate, photos)
Arrange and document adequate health insurance for all applicants
Complete any required health checks and obtain police certificates if requested
Create or log in to your ImmiAccount and fill in the online application form
Upload supporting documents and pay the application fee (current fee applies)
Monitor correspondence from the Department and respond promptly to any requests for further information

**Category 2.** Usually 1 year. This covers cities and major regional centres such as Adelaide, Perth, the Gold Coast, Newcastle, Wollongong, Hobart and Canberra. Some Category 2 areas in Tasmania are granted 2 years.
**Category 3.** Usually 2 years. This covers smaller regional centres and other regional areas.
A Post-Vocational Education Work 485 does not lead to this second visa.

blocks.x: The extra time is for building a later visa. Common next steps are a [491](/migrate-to-australia/skilled-work-regional-provisional-visa-subclass-491) if a state will nominate you, or an employer visa such as a [482](/employer-sponsored/sid-visa-482) or [494](/employer-sponsored/skilled-regional-494). seo.title: National Innovation Visa 858 Australia - Independent Talent Pathway | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: The National Innovation visa (subclass 858) is open. It is a permanent visa. You need an invitation before you can apply. It replaced the Global Talent visa.

intro: This permanent visa is open. It replaced the Global Talent visa on 6 December 2024. You send an expression of interest first. You can apply only if Home Affairs invites you. The old Global Talent pathway is closed.

blocks.x: The National Innovation visa is for people with an internationally recognised record of exceptional achievement in a profession, sport, the arts, or research. It is permanent. There is no points test and no employer sponsor. Send an expression of interest. It stays active for 2 years. If you are invited, apply within 60 days and include Form 1000 from a nominator. An expression of interest is not a visa application. See the [Home Affairs page](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/working-in-australia/visas-for-innovation/national-innovation-visa).
New applications for exceptional achievement use this visa. The older talent pathways are closed.

items.x: **Distinguished Talent visa (subclass 124).** This was the offshore distinguished talent visa. You cannot lodge a new subclass 124 application. Use the National Innovation visa.

**The previous Distinguished Talent visa (subclass 858).** The subclass number 858 is still used, but the old distinguished talent criteria are not. A new application is a National Innovation visa application, and you need an invitation first.

**Global Talent Independent program.** This closed on 6 December 2024. An old Global Talent expression of interest or unique identifier cannot be used to apply now. You need a new expression of interest for the National Innovation visa.

blocks.x: This is not a points-tested visa and it is not employer sponsorship. If your record is strong but not internationally recognised as exceptional, look at [skilled migration](/migrate-to-australia) or an [employer-sponsored visa](/employer-sponsored).

sections.name: Eligibility
sections.h2: Do You Have What It Takes?

items.x: You have an internationally recognised record of exceptional achievement, and you are still active in that field.
You have sent an expression of interest and Home Affairs has invited you to apply.
You apply within 60 days of the invitation.
A nominator with a national reputation in your field completes Form 1000. You include it with the application.
You can show you would be an asset to Australia and could establish yourself in your field.
You meet health and character requirements.
Permanent residence. You can live and work in Australia.
You can include eligible family members.
There is a pathway to citizenship once you meet the residence and character rules.
Read the [Home Affairs National Innovation visa page](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/working-in-australia/visas-for-innovation/national-innovation-visa).
Send an expression of interest. Wait for an invitation. Do not lodge a visa application before you are invited.
If you are invited, apply in ImmiAccount within 60 days. Include Form 1000 and pay the charge. The base charge is AUD 6,235.
**Initial Duration.** Permanent

blocks.x: Australian Citizenship Pathway

The National Innovation visa Subclass 858 provides permanent residency immediately upon grant, creating a direct and streamlined pathway to Australian citizenship for individuals with internationally recognized records of exceptional and outstanding achievement in professions, sports, arts, or academia and research. As a permanent resident through the National Innovation visa, you can pursue Australian citizenship after meeting the general residence requirement of four years lawful residence in Australia including at least 12 months as a permanent resident, demonstrating your ongoing commitment to contributing your exceptional talents to Australian society.

**There is no eligible nominator** where one is required.
